units.title: COLD BOOT
units.theme: Reconstructing what happened — and what used to happen

overview.intro: Every investigation starts with the log files. This node gives you the two tools you need to read your own past: the simple past for finished events on a timeline, and “used to” for the habits and states that were true for a long stretch of your life and are now closed. One is a single entry in the log; the other is a pattern in the data.
goals: Build affirmative, negative and interrogative sentences in the simple past with regular and irregular verbs.
Use was / were correctly with the right subject, including in questions and short answers.
Describe old habits and old states with used to / didn’t use to, and know when the simple past is the better choice.
overview.outcome: By the end you can give a three-minute account of a year of your life: what happened once, what you used to do every week, and what is no longer true.

vocab.def: to take place, to occur — usually without anyone planning it.
vocab.use: “Happen” has no passive: never “it was happened”. To ask about an event: “What happened?” with no auxiliary, because “what” is the subject.
examples: What happened at the meeting last night?
Something strange happened when I opened the file.
vocab.colloc: what happened · happen to someone · it happened suddenly

vocab.def: to see or realise something, often something small.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun, or by a that-clause: “I noticed that the door was open.” Different from “watch” (deliberate) — noticing is accidental.
examples: I noticed a car outside my building.
Nobody noticed that I left early.
vocab.colloc: notice a change · barely notice · you may have noticed

vocab.def: at that time in the past.
vocab.use: It works like a time marker for the simple past and for “used to”: “Back then, we used to walk everywhere.” Usually at the start or the end of the sentence.
examples: Back then I didn’t have a phone.
We were poor back then, but we were happy.
vocab.colloc: back then · way back then · back in those days

vocab.def: to change the place where you live.
vocab.use: “Move to” a new place, “move from” the old one, “move out of” a house: “We moved to Bogotá in 2019.”
examples: My family moved to another city when I was ten.
She moved out of her parents’ house last year.
vocab.colloc: move to a city · move away · move back home

vocab.def: the period of your life when you were a child.
vocab.use: An uncountable-feeling singular noun, normally with a possessive: “my childhood”, “her childhood”. “In my childhood” is correct but “when I was a child” sounds more natural.
examples: I spent my childhood in a small town.
Childhood memories are never complete.
vocab.colloc: a happy childhood · childhood friend · since childhood

vocab.def: a past habit or state that has now stopped.
vocab.use: Only exists in the past. Positive: “used to + verb”. Negative and question: “didn’t use to”, “Did you use to…?” — no final -d after “did”.
examples: I used to smoke, but I stopped two years ago.
Did you use to play football at school?
vocab.colloc: used to live · used to be · didn’t use to like

vocab.def: to stop doing something, usually a job or a habit.
vocab.use: Irregular and unchanging: quit – quit – quit. Followed by a noun or -ing: “I quit smoking.”
examples: He quit his job in March.
I quit going to the gym after the accident.
vocab.colloc: quit a job · quit smoking · quit halfway

vocab.def: before now; counting backwards from today.
vocab.use: Always goes AFTER the time period, and always with the simple past — never with the present perfect: “two years ago”, not “ago two years”.
examples: I met her three months ago.
We moved here a long time ago.
vocab.colloc: a while ago · long ago · not so long ago

vocab.def: very quickly and without warning.
vocab.use: Typically at the beginning of a narrative sentence to signal a break in the story: “Suddenly, the lights went out.”
examples: Suddenly everyone stopped talking.
The screen suddenly went black.
vocab.colloc: suddenly realise · all of a sudden · quite suddenly

vocab.def: something you remember; also your ability to remember.
vocab.use: Countable when it is one image from the past (“a memory of my grandfather”), uncountable when it is the mental ability (“a good memory”).
examples: I have a clear memory of that day.
My memory isn’t what it was.
vocab.colloc: a vivid memory · from memory · lose your memory

vocab.def: to think about something that happened in the past.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “Looking back on it, I made the right choice.” Inseparable.
examples: I look back on those years with a lot of affection.
Looking back, I should have said no.
vocab.colloc: look back on it · looking back · look back fondly

vocab.def: then, in that period — not now.
vocab.use: Marks a past judgement that has since changed: “At the time it seemed like a good idea.”
examples: At the time I didn’t understand why she left.
It was expensive at the time.
vocab.colloc: at the time · at that time · at the time it felt right

grammar.name: Simple past: ordinary verbs and the verb “to be”
grammar.short: I worked / I didn’t work / Did you work? — I was, they were.
grammar.rule: The simple past reports a finished action or a finished state at a known or implied point in the past. Ordinary verbs use the auxiliary “did” in negatives and questions, and the past form only in the affirmative. The verb “to be” never uses “did”: it changes its own shape into was / were.
form: Affirmative: subject + past form → She worked late. / They went home.
Negative: subject + didn’t + BASE verb → She didn’t work late. (never “didn’t worked”)
Question: Did + subject + BASE verb? → Did she work late?
To be: I / he / she / it WAS · you / we / they WERE → I was tired. They weren’t ready. Were you at home?
notes: The past form appears in ONE place only. Once “did” is present, the main verb goes back to its base form: “Did you see it?”, not “Did you saw it?”.
Regular verbs add -ed (worked, played). Spelling: consonant + y → -ied (study → studied); one-syllable CVC → double the consonant (stop → stopped).
Irregular verbs must be memorised in threes: go–went–gone, see–saw–seen, take–took–taken, buy–bought–bought.
“Was/were” carries the negative and the question by itself: “I wasn’t there”, “Were they late?” — adding “did” is always wrong.
Short answers repeat the auxiliary, not the verb: “Did you call?” — “Yes, I did.” / “Were you home?” — “No, I wasn’t.”
grammar.deep: Think of the simple past as a photograph rather than a video: it shows the event as one complete block, with a beginning and an end already inside it. That is why it lives so comfortably with closed time markers — yesterday, last week, in 2019, two years ago, when I was twelve. If the time is still open (this week, today, ever in my life) English prefers the present perfect instead, which is exactly the contrast you will meet at node 04. A second thing worth noticing: “to be” behaves differently because it is not an action, it is a link. Actions need a helper (“did”) to form questions; links can invert themselves (“Were you…?”). Learners who mix the two systems produce the classic error “Did you were at home?” — two auxiliaries competing for the same job. Choose one system per sentence: “did + base verb” for actions, “was/were” alone for states.

examples: I called you twice last night, but you didn’t answer.
Where did you go after the class?
She was in the office until nine and then she went home.
We weren’t ready, so the meeting started late.
grammar.watch: Never put a past form after “did” or “didn’t”, and never put “did” next to “was/were”. One past marker per clause is the whole rule.
more: I applied for three jobs last month and got two interviews.
She didn’t say anything, she just left.
Where did you go after the meeting?
They were already waiting when I arrived.
I wasn’t ready, so we started twenty minutes late.
Did anyone notice that the file was missing?

fix.right: I didn’t go to the office.
fix.why: After “didn’t” the verb returns to the base form.

fix.wrong: Did you was at the meeting?
fix.right: Were you at the meeting?
fix.why: “To be” makes its own past question; it never combines with “did”.

fix.wrong: When you arrived?
fix.right: When did you arrive?
fix.why: A wh-question with an ordinary verb still needs the auxiliary “did”.

drill.name: Three-part statement
drill.prompt: For each prompt, give a positive, a negative and a question in the simple past.

dialogue.line: Did you get my message yesterday?
No, I didn’t see anything. When did you send it?
Around six. I was still at the office.
That explains it — my phone was off until nine.

grammar.sound: Regular -ed has three sounds: /t/ after voiceless (worked), /d/ after voiced (called), /ɪd/ after t or d (wanted, decided). Only the third one adds a syllable.

grammar.name: Past habits and states with “used to”
grammar.short: I used to live here. Did you use to work nights?
grammar.rule: “Used to + base verb” describes something that was repeatedly true or permanently true in the past and is not true now. It always carries the idea of a contrast with the present. In negatives and questions it becomes “didn’t use to” and “Did … use to?”, with no final -d.
form: Affirmative: subject + used to + base verb → I used to work in a call centre.
Negative: subject + didn’t use to + base verb → I didn’t use to like coffee.
Question: Did + subject + use to + base verb? → Did you use to live in Cali?
Alternative negative (more formal): I never used to eat breakfast.
notes: “Used to” exists only in the past. For present habits use the present simple with an adverb of frequency: “I usually get up at six.”
It works for repeated actions (“I used to run every morning”) and for long states (“He used to be very shy”) — but never for a single event: “I used to break my leg” is wrong.
With a specific number of times or a fixed duration, use the simple past instead: “I went to Cartagena three times”, not “I used to go three times”.
Do not confuse it with “to be used to + -ing” (= to be accustomed to something), which is a different structure about familiarity, not about the past.
“Would” can also describe past habits in storytelling (“Every summer we would drive to the coast”), but it cannot describe past states: “He would be shy” does not mean he was shy.
grammar.deep: “Used to” is a comparison machine disguised as a tense. Every time you use it, your listener automatically hears the second half of the sentence even if you do not say it: “I used to smoke” means “…and I don’t now.” This is why it is so useful for talking about change — your city, your job, your body, your opinions. The pronunciation matters more than the spelling: in natural speech “used to” collapses into /ˈjuːstə/, one word, and the two t-sounds merge. That is also the reason the -d disappears after “did”: the sound was never really there. When you compare it with the simple past, remember the difference is not about truth but about framing. “I lived in Medellín for six years” and “I used to live in Medellín” report the same fact; the first frames it as one closed block of time, the second frames it as a former state that has been replaced by a new one.

examples: I used to hate vegetables when I was a kid.
Did you use to have long hair?
He didn’t use to talk much, but now he never stops.
There used to be a cinema on this corner.
grammar.watch: After “did”, write “use to” without the -d: “Did you use to smoke?” — and never combine it with a counted number of events.

She didn’t use to like coffee, and now she drinks four cups a day.
Did you use to walk to school?
There used to be a cinema on this corner.
We used to talk every week, but we lost touch.
I used to be terrified of flying.

fix.right: I used to live in Cali.
fix.why: The affirmative always keeps the -d: “used to”.

fix.wrong: I didn’t used to smoke.
fix.right: I didn’t use to smoke.
fix.why: After “did” the form goes back to “use to”.

fix.wrong: I used to go there yesterday.
fix.right: I went there yesterday.
fix.why: “Used to” describes a repeated past habit, never a single event.

drill.name: Then and not now
drill.prompt: Say one “used to” sentence and follow it immediately with the present reality.

dialogue.line: Did you use to live in this neighbourhood?
Yes, for about ten years. There used to be a market right here.
Really? What happened to it?
It closed in 2016. Now it’s a car park.

contrast.title: used to · would · simple past
rows: repeated habit or state, now over
I used to cycle to work.
repeated action only, in a story
Every summer we would visit my aunt.
There used to be a shop here.

grammar.sound: “Used to” is /ˈjuːstə/ — the d disappears entirely. Compare “I’m used to it” /ˈjuːstuː/, where the t is released.

speaking.text: Reconstruct last Saturday with your partner, hour by hour, using only the simple past. Then repeat the exercise for “a normal Saturday ten years ago” using “used to”.

One student is the investigator, one is the witness. The investigator asks eight past questions (four with “did”, four with “was/were”). The witness may lie once; the class guesses which answer was false.
Talk for ninety seconds about three things that used to be true about you and are not true now. End each one with “but now…”.

tips: If you hear yourself say “did” plus a past verb, stop and restart — one past marker per clause.
Learn irregular verbs in sound families: think–thought / bring–brought / buy–bought.
“Ago” only ever goes with the simple past: two years ago, not “I have gone two years ago”.

quiz.q: ___ you use to work at night when you lived in Bogotá?
quiz.explain: “Use to” takes the auxiliary “did”, and after “did” we write “use to” without the -d.

dynamics.name: Log file reconstruction
dynamics.how: Each group gets six scrambled events from one day (times included). They reconstruct the day in the simple past, then read it aloud while another group listens for missing “did”s and wrong past forms.
dynamics.payoff: Sustained simple-past narration with an audience whose only job is accuracy.

dynamics.name: Ten years ago
dynamics.how: Each student writes five “I used to…” sentences about ten years ago. Partners must respond to each with a present-tense contrast and one follow-up question in the simple past.
dynamics.payoff: Pairs the two grammar points of the node in a single exchange.

dynamics.name: Irregular verb ladder
dynamics.how: Teacher calls a base verb; the next student in line gives the past form and a full sentence. A wrong form sends the team back one rung on the board ladder.
dynamics.payoff: Irregular forms under time pressure, which is the only way they become automatic.

dynamics.name: True, false, used to
dynamics.how: Each student writes three past habits, one invented. The class questions them in the simple past — “Where did you work? How long did you stay?” — before voting.
dynamics.payoff: The interrogation forces the switch from “used to” into the simple past for details.

writing.title: Two paragraphs, ten years apart
writing.brief: Write about your life ten years ago and one specific day from that period. The first paragraph uses “used to” for habits and states; the second narrates the single day in the simple past.
criteria: At least three “used to” forms, all with the correct -d or base spelling.
The narrative paragraph contains one negative and one question in the simple past.
No “did” next to “was/were” anywhere in the text.

homework.title: Interview an older relative
homework.task: Ask someone at least twenty years older than you five questions about how their neighbourhood used to be. Write their answers in English: three sentences with “used to” and three in the simple past with a date or a time.

test.explain: After “didn’t” the verb returns to the base form.

test.explain: “You” takes “were”, and “to be” never uses “did”.

test.q: There ___ a cinema on this street.
test.explain: The affirmative form keeps the -d: “used to be”.

test.explain: An ordinary verb in a past wh-question needs the auxiliary “did”.

board: A timeline across the board with THEN on the left and NOW on the right.
Left column: used to + base (habits) | didn’t use to | Did you use to…?
Right column: simple past — did / didn’t + base, was / were.
A boxed model pair: “I used to walk to work. Yesterday I took the bus.”
Corner errors: “I didn’t went” and “Did you was?”

units.title: INVENTORY
units.theme: Counting what you have, and asking without pointing

overview.intro: Two very different skills share this node. First, quantity: English splits nouns into things you can count and things you can only measure, and each group takes a different set of quantifiers. Second, politeness: an indirect question hides the question inside a longer, softer sentence — the difference between demanding information and requesting it.
goals: Classify nouns as count or noncount and choose the right quantifier for each.
Ask how much / how many questions accurately.
Convert direct wh-questions into indirect questions with the correct word order.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe the contents of a kitchen, a budget or a hard drive with precise quantities, and ask a stranger five polite indirect questions.

vocab.def: how much there is of something you cannot count.
vocab.use: “Amount of + noncount noun”: an amount of money, of time, of data. For countable things use “number of”: “a number of files”.
examples: A huge amount of information was lost.
We spent a small amount of money on it.
vocab.colloc: a large amount of · the total amount · a fair amount of

vocab.def: a small quantity — “a few” for countable, “a little” for noncount.
vocab.use: With “a” they are positive (enough). Without “a” they turn negative: “few friends” means almost none; “little time” means not enough.
examples: I have a few questions and a little time.
Few people know the truth.
vocab.colloc: a few minutes · a little help · quite a few

vocab.def: more than enough.
vocab.use: Always with “of” before a noun, and it works for both count and noncount: “plenty of chairs”, “plenty of water”.
examples: Don’t rush — there’s plenty of time.
We have plenty of options.
vocab.colloc: plenty of time · plenty of room · plenty more

vocab.def: the box, bottle or bag that holds something.
vocab.use: Containers let you count uncountable things: a bottle of water, a bag of rice, a piece of advice.
examples: Buy two bottles of milk and a bag of sugar.
I need a container for the leftovers.
vocab.colloc: a plastic container · a piece of · a slice of

vocab.def: to want to know something; to ask yourself a question.
vocab.use: The classic opening for indirect questions: “I wonder where he lives.” Never invert after it.
examples: I wonder why she left so early.
I was wondering if you could help me.
vocab.colloc: I wonder if · I was wondering whether · make you wonder

vocab.def: the more formal alternative to “if” inside a reported question.
vocab.use: Use it when there are two options: “I don’t know whether to stay or go.” After a preposition, only “whether” is possible.
examples: Could you tell me whether the shop is open?
I’m not sure whether he got my message.
vocab.colloc: whether or not · whether to · it depends on whether

vocab.def: how much or how many of something there is.
vocab.use: More technical than “amount”. Common in shops and reports: “in large quantities”.
examples: We buy rice in large quantities.
The quantity is fine; the quality isn’t.
vocab.colloc: a small quantity · in quantity · quantity and quality

vocab.def: as much as you need.
vocab.use: Before a noun (“enough money”) but AFTER an adjective or adverb (“fast enough”, “good enough”).
examples: We don’t have enough chairs for everyone.
She isn’t old enough to drive.
vocab.colloc: enough time · not good enough · more than enough

vocab.def: to finish your supply of something.
vocab.use: Always with “of” before the noun. The thing that finishes is the object: “We ran out of milk.”
examples: We’ve run out of coffee again.
I ran out of time before the last question.
vocab.colloc: run out of money · run out of ideas · nearly run out

vocab.def: showing good manners and respect.
vocab.use: “It is polite to + infinitive”: “It’s polite to ask first.” The noun is “politeness”, the opposite is “rude”.
examples: It’s more polite to ask an indirect question.
He was very polite about my mistake.
vocab.colloc: polite request · perfectly polite · polite way of asking

vocab.def: two, or a small number of.
vocab.use: Countable nouns only, and always with “of”: “a couple of minutes”. Informal but extremely common.
examples: Give me a couple of minutes.
I sent a couple of emails about it.
vocab.colloc: a couple of days · a couple of things · just a couple

grammar.name: Expressions of quantity with count and noncount nouns
grammar.short: many files, much data, a few minutes, a little help.
grammar.rule: Countable nouns have a singular and a plural and answer “how many?”. Noncount nouns have no plural and answer “how much?”. The quantifier you choose must match the type of noun — and some quantifiers work with both.
form: Count only: many, a few, few, several, a number of, how many → many friends, a few ideas.
Noncount only: much, a little, little, a great deal of, an amount of, how much → much time, a little sugar.
Both: some, any, a lot of / lots of, plenty of, enough, no, all → a lot of people, a lot of money.
Make a noncount noun countable with a container or unit: two glasses of water, three pieces of advice.
notes: Noncount nouns take a singular verb: “The news is bad”, “Information is expensive”.
“Much” is rare in positive statements in modern spoken English; use “a lot of” instead: not “I have much work” but “I have a lot of work”.
“Some” in questions signals an offer or a request (“Would you like some coffee?”); “any” is for open questions and negatives (“Is there any coffee?”, “We don’t have any”).
Watch the frequent noncount traps: advice, information, furniture, luggage, homework, money, bread, work, traffic, research.
“A few / a little” are positive; “few / little” alone are negative and quite formal: “Few students passed” = a disappointing number.
grammar.deep: The count/noncount split is not really about physics — it is about how English decides to package a thing. Rice is made of countable grains, but English packages it as a mass; furniture is made of individual chairs, but English packages it as a mass too. That is why translation fails you here and lists have to be learnt. A useful test: put the word after “a” and after a number. If “an information” and “three informations” both sound impossible, the noun is noncount, and you need a unit word to count it — a piece of information, an item of furniture, a bit of advice. The second layer is register. “Much” and “many” survive comfortably in negatives and questions (“Do you have many friends?”, “There isn’t much time”), but in affirmative sentences they sound bookish, so speakers reach for “a lot of” and “plenty of”. Getting this right does more for how natural you sound than any single verb tense.

fix.right: She gave me two pieces of advice.
fix.why: “Advice” is noncount; count it with “piece(s) of”.

drill.prompt: For each noun, say whether it is count or noncount, then ask the matching “how much / how many” question.

dialogue.line: How many people have confirmed for Thursday?
Only a few so far — about six.
And how much time do we need for the setup?
Not much. Half an hour, and we don’t need many chairs.

grammar.sound: “A lot of” compresses to /əˈlɒtə/ and “a couple of” to /əˈkʌpləv/. The “of” never disappears, but it is never stressed.

grammar.name: Indirect questions from wh-questions (to be, do/does, can)
grammar.short: Where is it? → Could you tell me where it is?
grammar.rule: An indirect question wraps the real question inside an introductory phrase. Inside the wrapper, the word order goes back to normal statement order: the subject comes before the verb, and the auxiliaries “do / does / did” disappear completely.
form: Introducer + wh-word + subject + verb: Could you tell me where the station is?
With to be: Where is he? → Do you know where he is?
With do/does: Where does she work? → Can you tell me where she works?
With can: What can I do? → I’d like to know what I can do.
Yes/no questions use if or whether: Is it open? → Do you know if it’s open?
notes: Never invert twice: “Do you know where is the station?” is the most common error at this level — the inner clause is a statement, not a question.
When “do/does/did” disappears, the tense and the third-person -s move onto the main verb: “Where does he live?” → “…where he lives.”
If the whole sentence starts with a question (Could you tell me…?, Do you know…?) it takes a question mark; if it starts with a statement (I wonder…, I’d like to know…) it takes a full stop.
Common introducers: Could you tell me…, Do you know…, I wonder…, I’d like to know…, Do you have any idea…, Can you remember….
Indirect questions sound noticeably more polite, which is why they are the default with strangers, officials and customer service.
grammar.deep: Two grammars are colliding in these sentences, and only one of them can win. A direct question uses inversion — the verb jumps in front of the subject — because inversion is English’s way of marking “this is a question”. But in an indirect question the marking job has already been done by the introducer (“Could you tell me…”), so the inner clause no longer needs it and reverts to plain statement order. Think of it as a nested box: the outer box is the question, the inner box is a piece of information. Once you can see the inner clause as a noun-like chunk — “where he lives” is really just the name of a piece of information — the word order becomes obvious, because you would never invert inside a noun phrase. The politeness effect is worth naming too: by turning a demand into a report of your own curiosity, you give the other person room to decline, and English speakers read that space as courtesy.

fix.why: “If” replaces the inversion; the subject comes first.

drill.name: Wrap the question
drill.prompt: Turn each direct question into an indirect one using a different introducer each time.
items: How much is a single ticket?

dialogue.line: Excuse me, could you tell me where the ticket office is?
It’s on the left, past the café.
Thanks. And do you know what time it closes?
I’m not sure. I think it’s open until eight.

contrast.title: Direct → indirect
rows: Could you tell me where it is?
Do you know what it costs?
Do you know if it is free?
I was wondering if I can park here.
Do you know why she left?

grammar.sound: Indirect questions carry rising intonation on the wrapper, not on the inner clause: “Could you tell me↗ where the station is↘.”

speaking.text: In pairs, list what is in your fridge, your bag and your phone storage. Use at least six different quantifiers, and one container expression for each noncount noun.
One student works at an information desk; the other needs six pieces of information. Every question must be indirect. Any direct question loses a point.
The first student asks a direct question; the next converts it into an indirect one and adds a new direct question for the following student.

tips: Test a noun with “a” and a number — if both fail, it is noncount and needs a unit word.
Prefer “a lot of” in positive sentences and save “much/many” for questions and negatives.
In indirect questions, delete “do/does/did” and move the tense onto the main verb.

quiz.explain: Inside an indirect question the clause returns to statement order: subject (“the bus stop”) before the verb (“is”).

dynamics.name: Inventory audit
dynamics.how: Each group gets a picture of a cluttered room or storeroom and two minutes to look. Sheets away, then they write ten quantity statements from memory. Compare with the picture and score one point per accurate quantifier.
dynamics.payoff: Count/noncount choices under memory pressure, with the picture as the referee.

dynamics.name: Politeness upgrade
dynamics.how: Student A reads a blunt direct question from a card. Student B must rewrite it as an indirect question within five seconds. Roles swap every five cards.
dynamics.payoff: Speed builds the reflex of removing the inversion.

dynamics.name: Information desk
dynamics.how: Half the class staff a station, a clinic and a cinema with a fact sheet. The others circulate asking only indirect questions; any direct question gets sent to the back of the queue.
dynamics.payoff: Real information gap, and the penalty enforces the structure.

dynamics.name: Much or many auction
dynamics.how: Teacher reads a sentence with a gap. Teams bid points on their answer before hearing whether they are right, losing the bid if wrong.
dynamics.payoff: Betting makes learners commit publicly, which surfaces exactly who still guesses.

writing.title: An email to a service desk
writing.brief: Write an email asking a language school for information about a course. Ask four things using indirect questions, and describe your situation using at least four quantifiers.
criteria: Four indirect questions, all in statement order inside the clause.
Correct quantifier for each noun type — no “advices” or “much people”.
At least one “I was wondering if…” frame.

homework.title: Rewrite a real enquiry
homework.task: Find a form or web page in Spanish that asks for information. Write six indirect questions in English that would get the same information, then write four sentences about your own situation using a few, a little, plenty of and not enough.

test.q: Could you tell me where ___?
test.explain: Inside an indirect question the clause returns to statement order.

test.q: How ___ information did they give you?
test.explain: “Information” is noncount, so it takes “how much”.

test.q: She gave me two ___ of advice.
test.explain: Noncount nouns are counted with “piece(s) of”.

test.q: Do you know when the office ___?
test.explain: Drop “does” and restore the -s on the verb.

test.q: There were ___ people, so we finished quickly.
test.explain: “People” is countable, and “few” carries the negative meaning of almost none.

board: Two columns headed COUNT and NONCOUNT, filled from the class’s own examples.
Between them, the shared quantifiers: some, any, a lot of, plenty of, enough, no.
Under NONCOUNT, a counting strip: a piece of · a bit of · an amount of.
A transformation box: “Where is it?” → “Could you tell me where it is?”
Corner errors: “two advices” and “Could you tell me where is it?”

units.title: MIRROR
units.theme: Judging what things are like, and wishing they were different

overview.intro: This node is about evaluation. First you learn the machinery for saying that something is not good enough, too much, or as good as something else — with adjectives and with nouns. Then you learn the grammar of dissatisfaction: “wish”, the structure English uses to talk about the gap between reality and what you would prefer.
goals: Evaluate with too / enough / not … enough and compare with as … as.
Compare using nouns as well as adjectives (too much noise, not enough space).
Express present wishes with wish + past, and past regrets with wish + past perfect.
overview.outcome: By the end you can review a flat, a job or a city in detail and say three things you wish were different.

vocab.def: to say that you are not satisfied with something.
vocab.use: “Complain about + thing” or “complain to + person”: “I complained to the manager about the noise.”
examples: Everyone complains about the traffic here.
She complained that the room was too small.
vocab.colloc: complain about · a written complaint · nothing to complain about

vocab.def: full of too many people.
vocab.use: For places, not people: “a crowded bus”. The noun form is “crowd”; “crowds of people” is very common.
examples: The centre is too crowded on Saturdays.
It was so crowded that we left.
vocab.colloc: a crowded street · overcrowded · get crowded

vocab.def: easy and practical to use or reach.
vocab.use: For things and arrangements, not people: “a convenient location”. For people use “available”. Noun: convenience.
examples: The flat is convenient for the university.
Would Friday be convenient for you?
vocab.colloc: convenient location · at your convenience · not very convenient

vocab.def: money that you have to spend on something.
vocab.use: Countable when it is a specific cost (“travel expenses”), uncountable-feeling in “at great expense”. The adjective is “expensive”.
examples: Rent is my biggest expense.
We cut our expenses by half.
vocab.colloc: living expenses · a big expense · at your own expense

vocab.def: to want something that is not real, or that you cannot have.
vocab.use: Followed by a past form for a present regret: “I wish I had more time.” “Wish + to + infinitive” exists but is formal and means “want”.
examples: I wish I lived closer to work.
She wishes she could speak Japanese.
vocab.colloc: I wish I could · wish you well · make a wish

vocab.def: good enough; of an acceptable standard.
vocab.use: Very common in spoken evaluation: “a decent salary”, “a decent meal”. It means satisfactory, not excellent.
examples: It’s not luxury, but it’s a decent place to live.
He earns a decent wage.
vocab.colloc: a decent job · decent enough · perfectly decent

vocab.def: unwanted or unpleasant sound.
vocab.use: Noncount when general (“too much noise”), countable for one specific sound (“a strange noise”). Adjective: noisy.
examples: There’s too much noise from the street.
I heard a noise in the kitchen.
vocab.colloc: background noise · make a noise · noise pollution

vocab.def: the empty area available for something.
vocab.use: Both are noncount in this meaning: “not enough space”, “no room for another chair”. “A room” with the article means a bedroom or office.
examples: There isn’t enough space for a table.
Is there room for one more?
vocab.colloc: enough space · plenty of room · make room for

vocab.def: a disadvantage of something otherwise good.
vocab.use: Useful in balanced evaluation: “The main drawback is the price.” Opposite: advantage, benefit.
examples: The only drawback is the distance.
Every option has its drawbacks.
vocab.colloc: the main drawback · a serious drawback · drawbacks and benefits

vocab.def: to accept something unpleasant without complaining.
vocab.use: Three parts, always together, always with an object: “I can’t put up with it any more.”
examples: I can’t put up with the noise any longer.
She puts up with a lot at work.
vocab.colloc: put up with it · can’t put up with · have to put up with

vocab.def: almost, only barely.
vocab.use: Softens a judgement: “It’s just about big enough.” Different from “just” alone.
examples: The flat is just about big enough for two.
I just about finished on time.
vocab.colloc: just about enough · just about manageable

vocab.def: to accept something less good than you wanted.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun: “We settled for the cheaper one.” Carries mild disappointment.
examples: We settled for a smaller place near the centre.
I don’t want to settle for second best.
vocab.colloc: settle for less · settle for the cheaper option

grammar.name: Evaluations and comparisons with adjectives and nouns
grammar.short: too small, not big enough, as expensive as, too much noise.
grammar.rule: To evaluate, English measures a thing against a standard. “Too” says you are above the acceptable limit; “enough” and “not enough” say you are at or below it; “as … as” says two things are equal. The structure changes depending on whether the word after it is an adjective or a noun.
form: too + adjective → The flat is too small.
adjective + enough → The flat isn’t big enough.
too much / too many + noun → too much noise, too many people.
enough + noun → There aren’t enough parking spaces.
as + adjective + as → It’s as expensive as my old flat. / not as clean as…
as much / many + noun + as → It doesn’t have as much space as the other one.
notes: “Enough” goes BEFORE a noun but AFTER an adjective or adverb: “enough money”, “big enough”, “quickly enough”.
“Too” always means more than you want. It is never a synonym of “very”: “very big” can be good news; “too big” never is.
“Too much” goes with noncount nouns, “too many” with plurals — the same count/noncount split you met at node 02.
“Too + adjective + to + infinitive” compresses a whole evaluation: “It’s too far to walk.” The negative counterpart is “not … enough to”: “He isn’t old enough to drive.”
In negative comparisons both “not as … as” and “not so … as” are possible; the first is far more common in speech.
grammar.deep: Every evaluation has three hidden parts: the thing, the quality and the invisible standard. When you say “the room is too small”, you are not describing a size — you are reporting that the size fails a purpose you have in mind (small for what? for four people, for a desk). This is why native speakers so often finish an evaluation with an infinitive or a “for” phrase: “too small for a family”, “not quiet enough to work in”. Adding that second half makes your English sound analytical rather than merely negative. The adjective/noun distinction is mechanical but unforgiving: “too much expensive” and “too many noise” are both broken because “too much/many” only ever modifies nouns, while bare “too” only ever modifies adjectives and adverbs. Say the sentence in your head and ask what word comes next; that single question fixes almost every error in this structure.

chart.title: Choosing the right evaluation frame
rows: too much rent / too many bills

examples: This place is too far from the centre and it isn’t cheap enough.
There’s too much noise and not enough parking.
My new job isn’t as stressful as the old one.
It doesn’t have as many rooms as we wanted, but it’s convenient.
grammar.watch: “Enough” after adjectives, before nouns: “fast enough”, “enough time”. Never “enough fast”.
more: The flat is too far from the centre and it isn’t cheap enough.
There’s too much noise and not enough parking.
My new job isn’t as stressful as the old one.
This laptop is nearly as fast as yours, and half the price.
We had too many applicants and too little time.
The room is big enough, but it doesn’t have enough light.

fix.wrong: The room isn’t enough big.
fix.right: The room isn’t big enough.
fix.why: “Enough” follows an adjective and precedes a noun.

fix.wrong: There are too much people.
fix.right: There are too many people.
fix.why: “Too much” is for noncount nouns; countable plurals take “too many”.

fix.wrong: It’s not as expensive than the other one.
fix.right: It’s not as expensive as the other one.
fix.why: The “as … as” frame uses “as” both times; “than” belongs to comparatives.

drill.name: Three verdicts
drill.prompt: Judge each item three ways: with “too”, with “not … enough”, and with “as … as”.

dialogue.line: What did you think of the second flat?
It’s too far from the centre, and the kitchen isn’t big enough.
Is it cheaper than the first one?
Not really. It’s almost as expensive, with too much noise from the street.

grammar.sound: “Enough” is /ɪˈnʌf/ — the gh is an f. Stress the second syllable, or it will sound like “in a”.

grammar.name: Wishes
grammar.short: I wish I had more time. I wish I hadn’t said that.
grammar.rule: “Wish” talks about the distance between reality and what you want. To go one step away from reality, you move the verb one step back in time: a present wish takes a past form, and a past regret takes the past perfect.
form: Present / general wish: wish + past simple → I wish I lived alone. (I don’t.)
Present wish with “to be”: wish + were (all persons) → I wish I were taller.
Ability or possibility: wish + could → I wish I could drive.
Past regret: wish + past perfect → I wish I had studied more. / I wish I hadn’t sent that email.
Annoyance about someone else: wish + would → I wish you would listen.
notes: The past form after “wish” is not about past time — it signals unreality. “I wish I had a car” is about now.
“Were” is standard after “wish” for every person in careful English (“I wish she were here”), though “was” is common in informal speech.
“I wish I would…” is impossible for your own actions; use “could” or a simple past instead.
“Hope” and “wish” are not interchangeable: “hope” is for possible futures (“I hope you pass”), “wish” is for the impossible or the contrary-to-fact.
In the negative, the wish flips the reality: “I wish I hadn’t told him” means you did tell him and you regret it.
grammar.deep: “Wish” is your first encounter with the unreal past, the same machinery that later powers second and third conditionals at nodes 15 and beyond. English marks unreality by backshifting: one step back from the present gives you the past simple and means “not true now”; one step back from the past gives you the past perfect and means “not true then, and I cannot change it”. Notice how much emotional information the choice carries. “I wish I lived in Madrid” is a dream about the present; “I wish I had moved to Madrid” is regret about a decision. Learners often keep the tense in the present (“I wish I have more time”), which quietly destroys the meaning, because a present tense after “wish” claims the thing is real. Finally, “I wish you would…” deserves its own note: it is not really a wish at all but a polite complaint, and English speakers use it to criticise a repeated behaviour without saying “stop it”.

chart.title: Wish patterns and what they mean
rows: I wish I had a car.

examples: I wish I lived closer to the office — the commute is too long.
She wishes she had taken the other job.
I wish I could help you, but I’m busy all week.
I wish you wouldn’t leave the door open.
grammar.watch: After “wish”, never use a present tense: “I wish I had time”, not “I wish I have time”.
more: I wish I had more time for this.
I wish I were better at maths.
I wish I could come with you.
I wish I hadn’t sent that email.
She wishes she lived closer to her family.
I wish it would stop raining.

fix.wrong: I wish I have more time.
fix.right: I wish I had more time.
fix.why: A present wish moves the verb one step back into the past form.

fix.wrong: I wish I would be taller.
fix.right: I wish I were taller.
fix.why: For a present state, use “were”, not “would be”.

fix.wrong: I wish I didn’t say that.
fix.right: I wish I hadn’t said that.
fix.why: A regret about the past needs the past perfect.

drill.name: One step back
drill.prompt: Turn each true statement into a wish by moving the verb one step back in time.

dialogue.line: You look tired.
I am. I wish I had more time to sleep.
Can you change your shifts?
I wish I could. And honestly, I wish I hadn’t taken this job.

grammar.sound: “I wish I’d…” hides the past perfect in one sound: /aɪwɪʃaɪd/. Listen for the /d/ — it is the only clue that the regret is about the past.

speaking.text: Evaluate your neighbourhood in six sentences: two with “too”, two with “enough”, two with “as … as”. Then add one drawback you have to put up with.
Each student says one present wish and one past regret. The next student must react with a follow-up question before adding their own.
Two flatmates compare two apartments. One prefers A, the other B. Each must use nouns and adjectives in their comparisons and finish with a compromise.

tips: Finish an evaluation with a purpose (“too small for four people”) — it sounds far more natural.
“Too much” + noncount, “too many” + plural, plain “too” + adjective.
Backshift after “wish”: present wish → past form; past regret → past perfect.

quiz.q: The flat is nice, but it isn’t ___ for three people.
quiz.explain: “Enough” follows an adjective: big enough. “Too big” would mean the opposite problem.

dynamics.name: Flat viewing
dynamics.how: Four flat descriptions with prices and problems. The group must reject three and choose one, and every rejection must use “too”, “not enough” and one “as … as” comparison.
dynamics.payoff: Forces all three evaluation structures into a decision they actually have to reach.

dynamics.name: Wish chain
dynamics.how: Each student adds a wish that must use a different pattern from the person before — past simple, were, could, past perfect. Repeating a pattern sends you out.
dynamics.payoff: Prevents the class from collapsing into one favourite form.

dynamics.name: Goldilocks grading
dynamics.how: Given twelve objects and a context (a two-hour flight, a first day at work), pairs grade each as too much, not enough or just about right, and defend two of their calls to another pair.
dynamics.payoff: The defence stage generates the comparative frames spontaneously.

dynamics.name: Regret roleplay
dynamics.how: Student A describes a decision that went wrong. Student B must respond with three past-perfect wishes on A’s behalf, and A accepts or rejects each.
dynamics.payoff: Past-perfect wishes are the hardest form here; this gives them a reason to exist.

writing.title: The place I nearly took
writing.brief: Describe a place, job or course you considered and rejected. Explain what was wrong using “too” and “not enough”, compare it with what you chose using “as … as”, and finish with two wishes.
criteria: “Enough” placed correctly relative to adjectives and nouns.
One “too much” and one “too many”, each with the right noun type.
Two wishes with different patterns, one of them about the past.

homework.title: Six wishes, three tenses
homework.task: Write six wishes about your life: two about the present, two about ability, two about the past. Then rewrite each one as a plain true statement, so you can see the step back in time in every pair.

test.q: The flat is nice, but it isn’t ___ for three people.
test.explain: “Enough” follows an adjective.

test.q: There were too ___ applicants for one interview slot.
test.explain: “Applicants” is a countable plural, so “too many”.

test.q: I wish I ___ more time this week.
test.explain: A present wish takes the past simple.

test.q: I wish I ___ that message.
test.explain: A regret about a finished action takes the past perfect.

test.q: It isn’t as expensive ___ the first one.
test.explain: The frame is “as … as”; “than” belongs to comparatives.

board: A vertical scale: TOO MUCH at the top, JUST RIGHT in the middle, NOT ENOUGH at the bottom.
Beside it, the placement rule: ADJECTIVE + enough | enough + NOUN.
A “too” split: too much (noncount) | too many (count).
A wish ladder: wish + past simple · wish + were · wish + could · wish + past perfect.
Corner errors: “enough big” and “I wish I have”.

units.title: TIMELINE
units.theme: Closed time versus open time, and putting a story in order

overview.intro: This is the node where most learners either break through or plateau. The simple past and the present perfect describe the same events but frame time differently: one closes the file, the other keeps it open. Once that is clear, you learn the connectors that sequence a narrative so a listener can follow it without a map.
goals: Choose between the simple past and the present perfect according to the time frame.
Use ever, never, already, yet, just, since and for with the present perfect.
Order a story or a process with first, then, after that, next and finally.
overview.outcome: By the end you can tell your work or study history accurately, and explain a five-step process in clear sequence.

vocab.def: knowledge or skill you get from doing something; also an event you lived through.
vocab.use: Noncount for knowledge (“two years of experience”), countable for a single event (“a strange experience”).
examples: I have three years’ experience in customer service.
Moving abroad was an amazing experience.
vocab.colloc: work experience · from experience · a bad experience

vocab.def: up to now, in a period that is still open.
vocab.use: A classic present perfect signal: “I’ve read three chapters so far.” Usually at the end of the sentence.
examples: So far we haven’t had any problems.
How many have you finished so far?
vocab.colloc: so far so good · so far this year · nothing so far

vocab.def: used in negatives and questions for something expected but not done.
vocab.use: Goes at the end: “Have you finished yet?”, “I haven’t decided yet.” Never in affirmative sentences.
examples: I haven’t sent the report yet.
Has the package arrived yet?
vocab.colloc: not yet · haven’t yet · yet again

vocab.def: earlier than expected; before now.
vocab.use: Normally between “have” and the past participle: “I’ve already eaten.” In a question it shows surprise: “Have you already finished?”
examples: She has already left the office.
We’ve already seen that film.
vocab.colloc: already done · already there · already too late

vocab.def: to succeed in doing something after effort.
vocab.use: Takes a concrete object: achieve a goal, a result, success. Not used for objects you obtain: you achieve a goal, you get a car.
examples: She has achieved a lot in two years.
We achieved everything we planned.
vocab.colloc: achieve a goal · a great achievement · achieve success

vocab.def: one action in a sequence.
vocab.use: Instructions are built on it: “step by step”, “the first step”, “the next step is to + verb”.
examples: The first step is to open the file.
We did it step by step.
vocab.colloc: the next step · step by step · a big step forward

vocab.def: as the last thing; also after a long wait.
vocab.use: Two meanings. Sequencing: “Finally, add the sauce.” Relief: “He finally answered.” Not the same as “at the end”, which is about position.
examples: Finally, press Save.
They finally called me back.
vocab.colloc: and finally · finally arrive · finally over

vocab.def: “since” marks a starting point; “for” marks a duration.
vocab.use: Since 2019, since Monday, since I was a child · for three years, for a long time, for ages.
examples: I’ve worked here since March.
I’ve worked here for four months.
vocab.colloc: ever since · for ages · for the last two years

vocab.def: to search for information.
vocab.use: Separable: “look it up”, “look up the word”. The pronoun always goes in the middle.
examples: I looked up the address online.
If you don’t know it, look it up.
vocab.colloc: look up a word · look it up · look up the details

vocab.def: a short time ago; in the last few days or weeks.
vocab.use: Works with the present perfect (“I’ve recently moved”) and, when the moment is specific, with the simple past (“I saw him recently”).
examples: Have you seen her recently?
I’ve recently started a new course.
vocab.colloc: quite recently · until recently · recently published

vocab.def: to finally do something you have been delaying.
vocab.use: Followed by -ing: “I haven’t got round to calling them.” Very common in the negative perfect.
examples: I still haven’t got round to fixing it.
She finally got round to answering.
vocab.colloc: get round to it · never got round to it

vocab.def: until this moment, in a period that is still open.
vocab.use: A present perfect signal, like “so far”. Usually at the start or the end.
examples: Up to now, nobody has complained.
It has worked perfectly up to now.
vocab.colloc: up to now · up to this point

grammar.name: Simple past vs present perfect
grammar.short: I saw it yesterday. / I’ve seen it three times.
grammar.rule: The simple past places an event inside a finished period of time. The present perfect connects a past event to now: either the period is still open, or the result still matters, or the exact time is irrelevant.
form: Simple past: subject + past form (+ finished time) → I sent it yesterday.
Present perfect: subject + have/has + past participle → I have sent it.
Negative/question: I haven’t sent it. / Have you sent it?
Typical past markers: yesterday, last week, in 2020, two days ago, when I was young.
Typical perfect markers: ever, never, already, yet, just, so far, this week, since, for, recently.
notes: Once you name a finished time, the present perfect becomes impossible: “I have seen him yesterday” is always wrong.
Experience questions start in the perfect and continue in the past: “Have you been to Spain?” — “Yes, I went in 2019.”
“For” + duration and “since” + starting point both need the present perfect when the situation continues: “I’ve lived here for six years.”
News is announced in the present perfect and then developed in the simple past: “The company has hired a new director. She started on Monday.”
In American English the simple past sometimes replaces the perfect with “just” and “already” (“I just ate”); both are accepted, but the perfect is safer in exams.
grammar.deep: Try to stop asking “when did it happen?” and start asking “is the box closed?”. The simple past puts the event in a closed box: yesterday, last night, in 2019 — boxes you cannot add anything to. The present perfect puts the event in a box that is still on the table: today, this week, in my life so far — boxes where another event could still be added. That is why “I have written three emails today” makes sense (the day is not over) and “I have written three emails yesterday” does not. The second job of the present perfect is relevance: “I’ve lost my keys” tells you about a present problem, while “I lost my keys” is just a story. Because Spanish maps these tenses differently, the reliable strategy is not translation but signal-hunting: find the time expression in the sentence, decide whether it is open or closed, and let it choose the tense for you.

chart.title: Which tense does the time expression demand?
rows: I lived in Cali when I was a child.
Have you ever flown business class?

examples: I’ve worked in three companies, but I only stayed a year in the first one.
Have you finished the report yet? — Yes, I finished it this morning.
She has just left, so you missed her by two minutes.
We haven’t had any complaints so far this month.
grammar.watch: Finished time and the present perfect never share a sentence: “I have visited them last summer” must be “I visited them last summer”.
more: I’ve worked in three companies, but I only stayed a year in the first one.
Have you finished the report yet? — Yes, I finished it this morning.
She has just left, so you missed her by two minutes.
We’ve had four meetings about this and decided nothing.
I sent it on Tuesday and they replied the same day.
Nobody has said anything up to now.

fix.wrong: I have visited them last summer.
fix.right: I visited them last summer.
fix.why: Finished time and the present perfect cannot share a sentence.

fix.wrong: I finished it, so you can read it now — did you already see it?
fix.right: …have you already seen it?
fix.why: “Already” with a present result pulls the present perfect.

fix.wrong: How long do you work here?
fix.right: How long have you worked here?
fix.why: A situation that started in the past and continues takes the present perfect.

drill.name: Open then close
drill.prompt: Ask with the present perfect, then answer with the past simple and a finished time.

dialogue.line: Have you sent the invoice yet?
Yes, I sent it on Monday.
And have they replied?
Not yet. Up to now nobody has even opened the email.

contrast.title: Closed time or open time?
rows: today, this week, so far, up to now
I’ve worked here for two years.

grammar.sound: “Have” is nearly silent in fast speech: “Have you seen it?” becomes /əvjəˈsiːnɪt/. The clue is the participle, not the auxiliary.

grammar.name: Sequence adverbs: first, then, after that, next, finally
grammar.short: First… then… after that… finally.
grammar.rule: Sequence adverbs are signposts. They do not change the tense of the verb; they tell your listener where they are in the story or the process, and they are punctuated as introductory elements.
form: Opening: First, / First of all, / To begin with,
Middle: Then / Next / After that / Later / Meanwhile
Closing: Finally, / In the end, / Eventually,
With clauses instead of adverbs: After I finished, I called her. / Before leaving, check the door.
notes: “Then” is the only one that comfortably appears without a comma: “Then we ate.” The others usually take one when they open the sentence.
“After that” is a complete adverbial and needs no noun; “after” alone must be followed by a noun or clause: “after that” vs “after the meeting”.
Do not confuse “at the end” (position: at the end of the film) with “in the end” (result: in the end we stayed home) or “finally” (last in a list).
“Eventually” means after a long time or many difficulties — it is not simply the last item in a list.
Use “meanwhile” for two things happening at the same time: “Meanwhile, I was waiting outside.”
grammar.deep: Sequencing is where grammar becomes rhetoric. A speaker who marks their steps is easy to follow even when their vocabulary is limited, and a speaker who does not mark them sounds disorganised even with perfect verb forms. Two habits will make the difference. First, be consistent: if you open with “first”, close with “finally” — a list that begins and never ends leaves your listener waiting. Second, do not put a marker on every single sentence; three or four signposts in a paragraph is persuasive, one on every clause sounds like a recipe read aloud. Combining them with time clauses gives you variety: “First, I checked the log. After I found the error, I called the team. In the end, we restarted the server.” Notice that the sequence words carry the order, so the tenses can stay simple — that is exactly the point of them.

chart.title: Sequencing toolkit

examples: First, open the app. Then enter your code. After that, choose a plan. Finally, confirm.
We tried three suppliers. In the end, we went back to the first one.

grammar.watch: “In the end” = the final result; “at the end” = the final part of something. They are not interchangeable.

Then choose the file you want to upload.
After that, wait for the confirmation message.
Next, check that the name is correct.
Finally, close the window and log out.
In the end, we decided to postpone it.

fix.wrong: At first we ate, after we left.
fix.right: First we ate, then we left.
fix.why: “At first” means initially, in contrast to later; “after” needs a clause or a noun.

fix.wrong: Finally, I finally arrived at the end.
fix.right: Finally, I arrived.
fix.why: One closing signal per sentence; the rest is repetition.

fix.wrong: After that I checked it, I sent it.
fix.right: After I checked it, I sent it.
fix.why: “After that” is complete in itself; “after” introduces a clause.

drill.name: Five-step process
drill.prompt: Describe each process in exactly five steps, using a different sequence adverb for each step.

dialogue.line: How do I submit the form?
First, download it from the portal.
And then?
Then fill in section two, and after that scan it. Finally, email it to admin before Friday.

contrast.title: Sequencing words
rows: First, / First of all, / To begin with,

grammar.sound: Sequence adverbs take their own small intonation unit and a real pause: “First,‖ open the app.” Without the pause the signpost disappears.

speaking.text: Ask your partner about their experience: three present-perfect questions (Have you ever…?) followed by simple-past follow-ups (When did you…? Where was it?).
Explain a five-step process from your own life — cooking, commuting, a work task — using all five sequence adverbs, and no notes.
Say three present-perfect experience statements, one false. The group asks past-tense questions to find the lie.

tips: Hunt for the time expression first; it decides the tense for you.
Start with the perfect for experience, then switch to the past for details.
Open with “first” only if you plan to close with “finally”.

quiz.q: I ___ that film last weekend, and I’ve already seen it twice this year.
quiz.explain: “Last weekend” is finished time, so the simple past is required; the second clause has open time (“this year”) and takes the present perfect.

dynamics.name: Timeline triage
dynamics.how: Give sixteen sentence halves — eight time expressions, eight verb phrases. Groups must match them so that every sentence is grammatical, and justify any pair another group challenges.
dynamics.payoff: The challenge rule turns a matching exercise into an argument about the rule.

dynamics.name: CV interrogation
dynamics.how: Student A presents a short career history. Student B must ask five questions, opening each with the present perfect and following up in the simple past.
dynamics.payoff: The two-step is exactly what job interviews do, so the practice transfers directly.

dynamics.name: Process relay
dynamics.how: Each team member contributes one step of a process on the board, using a different sequence adverb. Any repeated adverb costs the team the round.
dynamics.payoff: Forces the whole toolkit instead of “then, then, then”.

dynamics.name: So far this year
dynamics.how: Students find three people who have done something they have not, then report back with one present perfect and one past simple sentence per person.
dynamics.payoff: The reporting stage puts both tenses side by side in third person.

writing.title: Progress report
writing.brief: Write a short update on a project, a course or a personal goal. Say what you have done so far, what you haven’t done yet, and narrate one specific step in the simple past with a date. Order the whole thing with sequence adverbs.
criteria: No finished time expression attached to a present perfect.
At least three different sequence adverbs, correctly punctuated.
One “so far” or “up to now” with a present perfect.

homework.title: Instructions, twice
homework.task: Write instructions for something you know how to do, in six steps with six different sequence adverbs. Then write four sentences about the last time you actually did it, using the simple past with real dates.

test.q: I ___ that film last weekend.
test.explain: “Last weekend” is finished time, so the simple past.

test.q: ___ you finished the report yet?
test.explain: “Yet” with a present result takes the present perfect.

test.q: She’s worked here ___ two years.
test.explain: “For” introduces a length of time; “since” a starting point.

test.q: ___, open the app and sign in.
test.explain: “First” opens a sequence; the others close it.

test.q: When ___ they arrive?
test.explain: A question asking for a specific time takes the simple past.
