units.title: FORECAST
units.theme: Plans and predictions, needs and advice

overview.intro: Two systems for talking about what is coming and what has to be done. “Be going to” and “will” both point at the future but come from different places — one from evidence and intention, the other from the moment of speaking. Then modals let you grade obligation, from a gentle suggestion to a non-negotiable requirement.
goals: Distinguish be going to (plan, evidence) from will (decision at the moment, prediction, promise).
Express degrees of necessity with have to, need to, must and don’t have to.
Give suggestions and advice with should, ought to, could and had better.
overview.outcome: By the end you can present a plan for the next six months and give a colleague graded advice about a decision.

vocab.def: to decide in advance what you are going to do.
vocab.use: “Plan to + infinitive” or “plan on + -ing”: “We plan to move in July.” Noun: a plan; “make plans”, not “do plans”.
examples: I’m planning to study abroad next year.
What are your plans for the weekend?
vocab.colloc: make a plan · according to plan · plan ahead

vocab.def: the time by which something must be finished.
vocab.use: “Meet a deadline” (succeed) or “miss a deadline” (fail). With “by”: “The deadline is by Friday” → better: “The deadline is Friday.”
examples: We have to meet the deadline on Friday.
The deadline has been moved to next week.
vocab.colloc: a tight deadline · meet the deadline · miss a deadline

vocab.def: probable; there is a good chance of it.
vocab.use: “Be likely to + verb” or “It’s likely that…”: “Prices are likely to rise.” The opposite is “unlikely”.
examples: It’s likely to rain this afternoon.
She’s unlikely to accept the offer.
vocab.colloc: highly likely · not likely · likely outcome

vocab.def: to need something as a rule or a condition.
vocab.use: More formal than “need”, common in rules: “The job requires two years’ experience.” Passive: “Applicants are required to…”.
examples: This position requires an advanced level of English.
You’re required to wear ID at all times.
vocab.colloc: a requirement · required by law · require attention

vocab.def: to tell someone about a danger or a problem in advance.
vocab.use: “Warn someone about something” or “warn someone (not) to do something”: “She warned me not to trust him.”
examples: I warned you about the traffic.
They warned us to arrive early.
vocab.colloc: a warning · warn against · fair warning

vocab.def: needing immediate attention.
vocab.use: For situations and tasks, not people: “an urgent problem”. Adverb: “urgently”. Noun: “urgency”.
examples: This is urgent — we need it today.
She urgently needs an answer.
vocab.colloc: urgent matter · nothing urgent · a sense of urgency

vocab.def: strong advice with a hint of consequence if you don’t follow it.
vocab.use: Always “had better + base verb”, contracted to “’d better”. Negative: “had better not”, never “hadn’t better”.
examples: You’d better call him before he leaves.
We’d better not be late again.
vocab.colloc: you’d better · had better not · I’d better go

vocab.def: responsible for a task or a group.
vocab.use: “In charge of + noun / -ing”: “She’s in charge of hiring.” Different from “responsible to”, which is about who your boss is.
examples: Who’s in charge of the schedule?
I’m in charge of training the new staff.
vocab.colloc: put someone in charge · in charge of a team · take charge

vocab.def: to move something to a later time.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “We postponed the meeting”, “postpone making a decision”. Informal equivalent: “put off”.
examples: They postponed the trip until August.
Let’s not postpone this any longer.
vocab.colloc: postpone a decision · indefinitely postponed · put off

vocab.def: a copy or an alternative in case the first one fails.
vocab.use: “A backup plan”, “make a backup”. As a verb it splits into two words: “back up your files”.
examples: We need a backup plan for Friday.
Did you back up the data?
vocab.colloc: backup plan · daily backup · back up the files

vocab.def: on the point of doing something, within minutes.
vocab.use: Followed by the base verb: “I’m about to leave.” Not used with a stated future time.
examples: I’m about to start the meeting.
We were about to leave when she called.
vocab.colloc: just about to · about to start

vocab.def: to arrive at a result you did not plan.
vocab.use: Followed by -ing or a place: “We ended up taking a taxi.”
examples: We ended up cancelling the whole trip.
I ended up paying twice.
vocab.colloc: end up doing · end up somewhere

grammar.name: Future with “be going to” and “will”
grammar.short: I’m going to study tonight. / I’ll help you.
grammar.rule: “Be going to” presents the future as already decided or already visible in the present: a plan you made before speaking, or evidence in front of you. “Will” presents the future as decided at this moment: an instant decision, an offer, a promise, or a personal prediction.
form: Going to: subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb → She’s going to look for a new job.
Will: subject + will + base verb → I’ll call you tonight. Negative: won’t.
Questions: Are you going to apply? / Will you be there?
Present continuous for fixed arrangements: I’m meeting the client at four.
notes: Prior intention takes “going to”; the decision existed before you spoke: “I’m going to sell my car.”
Spontaneous reaction takes “will”: the phone rings and you say “I’ll get it.”
Evidence in the present takes “going to”: “Look at those clouds — it’s going to rain.”
Offers, promises and refusals always take “will”: “I’ll help you”, “I promise I won’t forget”, “He won’t listen”.
For a fixed arrangement with a time and a place, the present continuous is often the most natural of the three: “We’re flying on Tuesday.”
grammar.deep: The two forms are not competing translations of one idea; they encode where the future comes from. “Be going to” is grammatically a present tense — literally “I am on my way to doing this” — so it always contains something that exists now: your intention, or evidence you can point at. “Will” contains no present at all, which is why it fits the instant of speaking so well: decisions taken as you speak, offers made as you make them, predictions based on nothing but your own opinion. Two consequences follow. First, in a prediction with visible evidence, “going to” is stronger: “She’s going to fall!” is what you shout when you see her slipping. Second, in the main clause of a first conditional (node 09) English prefers “will”, because that future is generated by a condition rather than by a present plan. When both feel possible, ask yourself: did I decide this before I opened my mouth? If yes, “going to”.

chart.title: Which future form?
rows: I’m going to take a course.
I’ll drive you. / I won’t tell anyone.

examples: I’m going to start the course in September — I already paid for it.
That box looks heavy. I’ll give you a hand.
Look at the queue. We’re going to be late.
Don’t worry, I won’t say anything to her.
grammar.watch: After “will” and after “going to”, the verb stays in the base form: “I will call”, “I’m going to call” — never “to call” or “calling”.
more: I’m going to start the course in September — I already paid for it.
That box looks heavy. I’ll give you a hand.
Look at the queue. We’re going to be late.
Don’t worry, I won’t forget.
She’s going to hand in her notice next week.
I think it’ll be quieter after seven.

fix.wrong: I will start the course in September, I already paid.
fix.right: I’m going to start the course in September.
fix.why: A decision made before speaking takes “going to”.

fix.wrong: We going to be late.
fix.right: We’re going to be late.
fix.why: “Going to” always keeps am / is / are.

fix.wrong: I’ll to call you tonight.
fix.right: I’ll call you tonight.
fix.why: After “will” the verb stays in the base form.

drill.name: Plan or offer
drill.prompt: For each situation give one “going to” sentence (a plan or visible evidence) and one “will” sentence (a decision made now).
items: a heavy bag on the floor

dialogue.line: What are you going to do about the deadline?
I’m going to ask for two more days — I decided last night.
Do you want help with the figures?
Would you? Then I’ll finish the text tonight.

grammar.sound: “Going to” becomes /ˈɡənə/ and “will” hides inside the pronoun: “I’ll” /aɪl/, “he’ll” /hiːl/. Recognise them at speed even if you say the full forms.

grammar.name: Modals for necessity and suggestion
grammar.short: You have to register. You should rest. You’d better hurry.
grammar.rule: Modals grade how strong an idea is. For necessity English runs from “must / have to” (no choice) through “need to” (practical necessity) to “don’t have to” (free choice). For advice it runs from “could” (an option) through “should / ought to” (recommendation) to “had better” (urgent, with a consequence).
form: Necessity: must / have to / need to + base verb → You have to show your ID.
No necessity: don’t have to / don’t need to → You don’t have to pay in advance.
Prohibition: mustn’t / can’t → You mustn’t use your phone here.
Advice: should / shouldn’t / ought to / had better (not) → You should get some sleep.
Weak suggestion: could / might want to → You could ask your manager first.
notes: “Mustn’t” and “don’t have to” are opposites, not synonyms: “You mustn’t tell her” = it is forbidden; “You don’t have to tell her” = it is optional. This is the single most valuable distinction in this node.
“Have to” speaks about external rules (the law, your boss, the schedule); “must” often sounds like the speaker’s own authority and is more common in written notices than in conversation.
Modals have no -s, no “to” and no “do”: “She should call”, “Should I call?”, never “She shoulds” or “Does she should”.
“Have to” is the only one that conjugates and has all tenses: had to, will have to, has to.
“Had better” is stronger than “should” and implies a bad outcome if the advice is ignored: “You’d better leave now or you’ll miss it.”
grammar.deep: Think of these modals as a volume dial rather than a list of words. On the necessity dial, “must” and “have to” are at maximum, “need to” slightly below, “should” is a recommendation, “could” is barely a suggestion, and “don’t have to” switches the dial off entirely. Speakers move along the dial for social reasons, not grammatical ones: telling your boss “you must send this” is a serious face-threat, while “you might want to send this” says the same thing without cost. The negative side is where meanings flip rather than fade, so it repays memorising as pairs: must → mustn’t (forbidden), have to → don’t have to (optional), should → shouldn’t (bad idea), had better → had better not (warning). One last structural note: because true modals never change form, all the tense work is done by “have to” — “I had to work yesterday”, “I’ll have to work tomorrow” — which is why it survives in real speech far more than “must”.
examples: You have to bring your ID, but you don’t have to pay anything.
You mustn’t share this password with anyone.
You should talk to her before the meeting — you ought to explain your side.
We’d better book now; the flights are filling up.
grammar.watch: “Don’t have to” is freedom; “mustn’t” is prohibition. Mixing them changes your meaning completely.
more: You have to show your ID at reception.
You don’t have to pay in advance.
You mustn’t leave the door unlocked.
You should rest for a couple of days.
You’d better hurry — it closes at six.
We need to book before the end of the month.

fix.wrong: You mustn’t wear a suit — the office is casual.
fix.right: You don’t have to wear a suit.
fix.why: “Mustn’t” is a prohibition; the absence of obligation is “don’t have to”.

fix.wrong: You should to rest.
fix.right: You should rest.
fix.why: Modals take the base verb with no “to”.

fix.wrong: You had better to hurry.
fix.right: You’d better hurry.
fix.why: “Had better” is followed directly by the base verb.

drill.name: Grade the pressure
drill.prompt: Say the same idea three ways: as an obligation, as advice, and as no obligation at all.

dialogue.line: Do I have to register before Friday?
You don’t have to, but you should — the places fill up.
And the deposit?
That you do have to pay. And you mustn’t send cash by post.

contrast.title: Grading necessity
rows: don’t have to / don’t need to

grammar.sound: “Have to” is /ˈhæftə/ and “has to” is /ˈhæstə/ — the v turns into an f. “Mustn’t” drops the first t completely: /ˈmʌsnt/.

speaking.text: Present your plan for the next six months in one minute: three sentences with “going to”, two predictions with “will”, one fixed arrangement in the present continuous.
One student describes a real problem. Three others respond, each at a different volume: “you could…”, “you should…”, “you’d better…”. The group ranks which was most appropriate.
In pairs, write the six rules of a place you know using must, mustn’t, have to and don’t have to. Read them out; the class guesses the place.

tips: Decided before you spoke? “Going to”. Deciding as you speak? “Will”.
“Don’t have to” ≠ “mustn’t” — check which one you really mean.
Only “have to” can change tense; “must” has no past of its own.

quiz.q: You ___ wear a suit — the office is completely casual.
quiz.explain: There is no obligation, so “don’t have to”. “Mustn’t” would mean suits are forbidden.

dynamics.name: Forecast panel
dynamics.how: Each group makes six predictions about the next month — three from visible evidence (“going to”) and three from opinion (“will”) — then defends the split to another group.
dynamics.payoff: The defence forces learners to articulate why each form was chosen.

dynamics.name: Rules of the building
dynamics.how: Invent the rules for a shared workspace: three obligations, three prohibitions, two things residents don’t have to do, and two pieces of advice. Post them and let other groups hunt for wrong modals.
dynamics.payoff: The mustn’t / don’t have to contrast has to be got right or the poster reads absurdly.

dynamics.name: Instant offers
dynamics.how: Teacher describes a small crisis. Students must respond within three seconds with a “will” offer. Hesitation passes the turn on.
dynamics.payoff: “Will” for on-the-spot decisions becomes reflexive rather than translated.

dynamics.name: Advice auction
dynamics.how: Read a dilemma. Teams write advice using should, ought to or had better; the class votes for the best and the winning team explains their modal choice.
dynamics.payoff: Grades advice by strength, which is what learners usually flatten.

writing.title: Two weeks ahead
writing.brief: Write about the next two weeks: three things you are going to do and why, two predictions with “will”, and three rules or obligations you are under — including one thing you don’t have to do.
criteria: “Going to” for decided plans, “will” for predictions and offers — no mixing.
One “don’t have to” with a clearly optional action.
No “to” after any modal.

homework.title: House rules, real ones
homework.task: Write the real rules of a place you know — your home, your workplace, your gym — in eight sentences using must, have to, don’t have to, mustn’t and should. Mark which two you personally break.

test.q: You ___ wear a suit — the office is completely casual.
test.explain: There is no obligation, so “don’t have to”.

test.q: Look at those clouds. It ___ rain.
test.explain: A prediction from present evidence takes “going to”.

test.q: That bag looks heavy. ___ carry it for you.
test.explain: An offer decided at the moment of speaking takes “will”.

test.q: You ___ leave the door unlocked.
test.explain: This is a prohibition, so “mustn’t”.

test.q: You’d better ___ now — it closes at six.
test.explain: “Had better” is followed by the base verb.

board: Two future boxes: GOING TO (decided / evidence) | WILL (decided now / prediction / offer).
Under them, the never-forget note: keep am / is / are with “going to”.
A pressure gauge from MUST at the top to DON’T HAVE TO at the bottom, with should and had better marked.
A boxed contrast: “You mustn’t smoke.” ≠ “You don’t have to smoke.”
Corner error: “You should to rest.”

units.title: HANDSHAKE
units.theme: Two-part verbs and the art of asking someone to do something

overview.intro: A handshake is a protocol: a request, a response, an agreement. This node gives you the everyday verbs that come in two parts — turn off, pick up, put away — and the polite frames English uses to ask for a favour, including the one that famously inverts your answer: “Would you mind…?”
goals: Use separable and inseparable two-part verbs with the right word order.
Respond to requests with will, sure, of course and I’m afraid I can’t.
Make and answer requests with can, could, would and Would you mind + -ing.
overview.outcome: By the end you can ask for six different favours at three levels of politeness, and respond to requests naturally in either direction.

vocab.def: to stop or start a machine, light or tap.
vocab.use: Separable: “turn off the light” or “turn the light off”; with a pronoun the middle is obligatory: “turn it off”.
examples: Could you turn off the air conditioning?
Turn it on and see if it works.
vocab.colloc: turn off the lights · turn on the news · turn it off

vocab.def: to lift something; to collect a person or thing; to answer a call.
vocab.use: Separable, with several meanings. Context decides: “pick up the kids”, “pick up the phone”, “pick up a habit”.
examples: Can you pick me up at eight?
Nobody picked up when I called.
vocab.colloc: pick up the phone · pick someone up · pick up speed

vocab.def: to return something to its usual place.
vocab.use: Separable. Different from “put off” (postpone) and “put up with” (tolerate).
examples: Please put your things away before you leave.
She put away the dishes.
vocab.colloc: put the tools away · put it away · put away savings

vocab.def: to take care of someone or something.
vocab.use: Inseparable: the object always comes after “after”: “look after the baby”, “look after her” — never “look her after”.
examples: Could you look after my dog this weekend?
Who looks after the accounts?
vocab.colloc: look after children · look after yourself · someone to look after it

vocab.def: to write the required information on a form.
vocab.use: Separable, and both particles are correct (“out” is more American, “in” more British).
examples: Fill out this form and hand it in at reception.
Have you filled it in yet?
vocab.colloc: fill out a form · fill in the blanks · fill it out

vocab.def: a helpful action you do for someone because they ask.
vocab.use: “Do someone a favour”, “ask a favour”. The set opener “Can you do me a favour?” prepares your listener for a request.
examples: Can you do me a favour and check this?
She asked me for a favour.
vocab.colloc: do me a favour · a big favour · return the favour

vocab.def: to be annoyed or bothered by something.
vocab.use: “Would you mind + -ing” is a request; “I don’t mind” means it is fine with you. Answering “yes” to “Would you mind…?” is a refusal.
examples: Would you mind closing the window?
I don’t mind waiting.
vocab.colloc: would you mind · never mind · I don’t mind at all

vocab.def: a softener before bad news or a refusal.
vocab.use: Never about fear here: “I’m afraid I can’t” is the standard polite “no”. It comes before the bad news.
examples: I’m afraid I can’t help you today.
I’m afraid the shop is closed.
vocab.colloc: I’m afraid not · I’m afraid so · I’m afraid I can’t

vocab.def: to give work or a document to a person in authority.
vocab.use: Separable: “hand in your report”, “hand it in”. Compare “hand out” = distribute to many people.
examples: Hand in your forms by Friday.
She handed it in late.
vocab.colloc: hand in homework · hand in your notice · hand it in

vocab.def: immediately.
vocab.use: A natural way to accept a request: “I’ll do it right away.” Synonyms: at once, straight away.
examples: I’ll send it right away.
He answered right away.
vocab.colloc: right away · straight away · not right away

vocab.def: to solve a problem or organise something messy.
vocab.use: Separable: “sort out the files”, “sort it out”. Very common in spoken British English.
examples: Can you sort out the seating for Friday?
Don’t worry, I’ll sort it out.
vocab.colloc: sort it out · sort out a problem · get sorted

vocab.def: to reply to someone later.
vocab.use: Inseparable, with a person: “I’ll get back to you tomorrow.” Standard in work requests.
examples: I’ll get back to you as soon as I know.
She never got back to me.
vocab.colloc: get back to you · get back to me on that

grammar.name: Two-part verbs and “will” for responding to requests
grammar.short: Turn it off. — Sure, I’ll do it right now.
grammar.rule: A two-part (phrasal) verb is a verb plus a particle whose meaning is often unpredictable from its parts. Separable verbs allow the object between the two parts and force it there when the object is a pronoun; inseparable verbs never split. When you agree to a request, English answers with “will”, because the decision is made at that moment.
form: Separable, noun object: turn off the light / turn the light off.
Separable, pronoun object: turn it off (obligatory middle position).
Inseparable: look after the baby / look after her (never split).
Three-part: put up with the noise, run out of milk — never split.
Responses: Sure, I’ll do it. / Of course, I’ll take care of it. / I’m afraid I can’t right now.
notes: The pronoun rule is the one to automate: “pick it up”, “turn them on”, “fill it out”. “Pick up it” is always wrong.
Three-part verbs behave like inseparable verbs because the second particle is really a preposition: “I can’t put up with it.”
Many two-part verbs have a one-word formal equivalent — put off / postpone, find out / discover, hand in / submit. Choose according to register.
Agreeing to a request uses “will”, not the present: “I’ll do it now”, not “I do it now”.
Softening a refusal is expected in English: give a reason after “I’m afraid I can’t” or you will sound abrupt.
grammar.deep: Phrasal verbs are the reason fluent English sounds informal even when the topic is serious, and the reason careful learners can sound stiff. The grammar has exactly two moving parts. The first is separability, which you cannot deduce — you have to notice it — but the pronoun test settles it instantly: if “turn it off” sounds right, the verb separates; if only “look after it” works, it does not. The second is meaning, and here the particle is not decoration. “Up” often adds completion (drink up, fill up), “off” often adds disconnection (turn off, call off), “out” often adds distribution or discovery (hand out, find out). Learning them in families rather than alphabetically means you can guess new ones. On the response side, notice that English almost never answers a request with a bare “yes”: the pattern is agreement word plus “will” plus the action — “Sure, I’ll send it right away” — and that little formula will make you sound cooperative in a way “yes” alone never does.

grammar.name: Requests with modals and “Would you mind…?”
grammar.short: Can you help? Could you help? Would you mind helping?
grammar.rule: English grades politeness in requests by distance. “Can you” is direct and friendly, “Could you” and “Would you” add distance and therefore courtesy, and “Would you mind + -ing” is the most indirect because it asks about the other person’s feelings rather than their actions.
form: Can / Could / Will / Would you + base verb? → Could you open the window?
Would you mind + -ing? → Would you mind opening the window?
Would you mind if I + past? → Would you mind if I opened the window?
Accepting: Sure. / Of course. / No problem. / Not at all. / I’d be happy to.
Declining: I’m afraid I can’t… / Sorry, but… / I’d rather not, because…
notes: “Would you mind” is followed by -ing, never an infinitive: “Would you mind waiting?”, not “to wait”.

The answers are inverted: “No, not at all” means yes, I will do it; “Yes, I would mind” is a refusal. Because this confuses everyone, speakers usually reply with “Sure” or “Of course” plus the action.
“Would you mind if I…” asks permission for yourself and takes a past form (“if I borrowed your charger”); “Would you mind + -ing” asks the other person to act.
Longer requests are politer: adding “possibly”, “just” or a reason increases the courtesy (“Could you possibly send it today? I need it for the meeting.”).
“Can you” is not rude among friends and colleagues — over-formality with people you know well can sound cold or sarcastic.
grammar.deep: Politeness in English is not a set of magic words but a strategy of leaving the other person an exit. Each step up the scale widens that exit. “Open the window” gives none. “Can you open the window?” asks about ability, which is easy to refuse in theory. “Could you” shifts into the hypothetical, so the request is one step removed from reality. “Would you mind opening the window?” does not even ask about the action — it asks whether the action would bother you, which is why the polarity of the answer flips: you are literally answering the question “is this a problem?”. Learners lose points in two opposite directions here. Some stay at the direct end and sound demanding; others use maximum politeness with close friends and sound distant. Match the level to the size of the favour and the closeness of the relationship, and always give a reason when you refuse — in English, a bare “no” is heard as a rebuke.

units.title: PAYLOAD
units.theme: What things are for, and telling people how to do them

overview.intro: A payload has a purpose. This node is about expressing purpose and function — what a tool is for, why you do something — using infinitives and gerunds, and then about giving clear instructions and suggestions with imperatives and infinitive structures.
goals: Describe purpose with “to + verb”, “in order to” and “for + -ing”.
Choose correctly between an infinitive and a gerund after a verb, an adjective or a preposition.
Give instructions with imperatives and suggestions with infinitive patterns.
overview.outcome: By the end you can explain what any object or app is for, and give a set of clear instructions that a stranger could follow.

vocab.def: the reason why something exists or is done.
vocab.use: “The purpose of X is to + verb”. “On purpose” means deliberately, which is a different meaning.
examples: The purpose of this form is to collect your data.
He did it on purpose.
vocab.colloc: the main purpose · for this purpose · serve a purpose

vocab.def: to have a particular function.
vocab.use: Two patterns: “It’s used for storing files” (+ -ing) or “It’s used to store files” (+ infinitive). Both are correct.
examples: This app is used for editing photos.
A password manager is used to store keys safely.
vocab.colloc: widely used for · what’s it used for · used to do something

vocab.def: a more formal way of saying “to” when giving a reason.
vocab.use: “In order to + verb” and the negative “in order not to + verb”, which is the standard way to express a negative purpose.
examples: I left early in order to avoid the traffic.
She whispered in order not to wake the baby.
vocab.colloc: in order to · in order not to · so as to

vocab.def: a piece of equipment made for a particular job.
vocab.use: Countable and slightly technical: “a mobile device”, “a safety device”. Everyday alternative: “gadget”.
examples: This device measures air quality.
Turn off all electronic devices.
vocab.colloc: a smart device · a safety device · mobile devices

vocab.def: to stay away from something, or stop it from happening.
vocab.use: Always followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “avoid making mistakes”, not “avoid to make”.
examples: Avoid clicking on strange links.
I left early to avoid the queue.
vocab.colloc: avoid a problem · hard to avoid · avoid doing something

vocab.def: the steps that tell you how to do something.
vocab.use: Usually plural: “follow the instructions”. “An instruction” alone is rare and formal.
examples: Read the instructions before you start.
He gave us clear instructions.
vocab.colloc: follow instructions · clear instructions · instruction manual

vocab.def: to check that something is true or done.
vocab.use: Followed by a clause: “Make sure you save it.” Also “make sure of + noun”. Extremely common in instructions.
examples: Make sure the door is locked.
Make sure you back up your files first.
vocab.colloc: make sure · just to make sure · make sure of it

vocab.def: an object or program used to do a job.
vocab.use: Physical and digital: “a search tool”, “the right tool for the job”.
examples: This is the best tool for the job.
We use an online tool to track hours.
vocab.colloc: a useful tool · power tools · the right tool

vocab.def: good enough to justify the time or money.
vocab.use: “Worth + -ing”: “It’s worth trying.” Never an infinitive: not “worth to try”.
examples: It’s worth checking the price online.
The trip was worth every peso.
vocab.colloc: worth doing · well worth it · not worth the trouble

vocab.use: Followed only by -ing: “keep trying”, “keep asking”. “Keep on + -ing” adds insistence.
examples: Keep pressing the button until it beeps.
He keeps forgetting his password.
vocab.colloc: keep going · keep trying · keep on asking

vocab.use: Usually future or present perfect: “That will come in handy.” Not used of people.
examples: Take the adapter — it might come in handy.
That course has come in handy more than once.
vocab.colloc: come in handy · might come in handy

vocab.def: the purpose or reason for something.
vocab.use: Followed by -ing or a noun: “What’s the point of waiting?” Often in rhetorical questions.
examples: What’s the point of buying two?
The whole point of the app is speed.
vocab.colloc: the point of it · there’s no point in waiting

grammar.name: Infinitives and gerunds for uses and purposes
grammar.short: It’s used to open files. / It’s used for opening files.
grammar.rule: To express purpose, English offers an infinitive (“to + verb”) or a preposition plus a gerund (“for + -ing”). Which one you use depends on the frame: after most verbs and after “in order”, use the infinitive; after any preposition, use the gerund.
form: Purpose with infinitive: I called to confirm the time. / in order to confirm / so as to confirm.
Negative purpose: in order not to / so as not to → I left early so as not to miss it.
Function with for + -ing: This key is for opening the back door.
Verb + gerund: enjoy, avoid, keep, finish, mind, suggest, recommend → I avoid using public Wi-Fi.
Verb + infinitive: want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, try → We decided to change the password.
Preposition + gerund (always): interested in learning, good at fixing, instead of waiting, before leaving.
notes: “For + verb” is impossible: never “for to open” or “I came for see you”. Use “to open”, “to see you”.

After every preposition the verb takes -ing. “To” is sometimes a preposition (look forward to seeing you) and sometimes an infinitive marker (want to see you) — this is why that pair confuses learners.
A few verbs take either form with almost no change: begin, start, continue, like, love, hate. A few change meaning: “I stopped smoking” (quit) vs “I stopped to smoke” (paused in order to).
“Remember / forget” follow the same logic: “remember to lock the door” (a task ahead) vs “remember locking the door” (a memory behind).
Both function patterns are correct and common: “used to store data” and “used for storing data”. Choose one and stay consistent inside a sentence.
grammar.deep: Behind the lists there is one reliable principle: the infinitive looks forward, and the gerund names a thing. “To + verb” carries intention, direction and futurity, which is why it fits purpose (“I came to help”), plans (“I hope to travel”) and needs (“I need to sleep”). The gerund turns an action into a noun, which is why it fits after prepositions (a preposition always needs a noun-like object) and after verbs that talk about experiencing an action rather than aiming at it (enjoy, avoid, finish, mind). Test any doubtful case by substituting a noun: “I’m interested in coffee” works, so “interested in learning” must take -ing; “I want a coffee” works too, but “I want to learn” aims at something not yet real. Once you feel that difference, the small group of verbs that take both stops being a contradiction: they simply allow you to choose between naming an activity and aiming at a result.

grammar.name: Imperatives and infinitives for giving suggestions
grammar.short: Check the cable. / Try restarting it. / It’s a good idea to back up.
grammar.rule: The imperative is the base verb with no subject, used for instructions, directions and warnings. For suggestions, English softens the imperative with introductory phrases and infinitive structures so that advice does not sound like an order.
form: Imperative: Open the app. / Don’t click that link. / Never share your password.
Softened imperative: Please check…, Just press…, Try pressing…, Make sure you save…
Infinitive suggestion: It’s a good idea to arrive early. / The best thing to do is to call them.
Verb + object + infinitive: I advise you to wait. / I’d recommend you to ask (or: I’d recommend asking).
Let’s + base verb for shared suggestions: Let’s try again tomorrow.
notes: Imperatives have no subject, but you can add one for emphasis or contrast: “You sit here, and you take that side.”
Bare imperatives are normal in written instructions and recipes, and normal between friends, but they can sound abrupt in a request to a stranger — soften with “please”, “just”, or a modal.
“Try + -ing” suggests an experiment (“try restarting it”); “try + to” suggests effort against difficulty (“try to stay calm”).
“Recommend” and “suggest” are never followed by an object plus infinitive in careful English: say “I suggest waiting” or “I suggest that you wait”, not “I suggest you to wait”.
Negative imperatives always use “don’t”, even with “be”: “Don’t be late.”
grammar.deep: Instructions and suggestions are the same content at two different social temperatures. The imperative is maximally efficient — no subject, no modal, no hedge — which is exactly why manuals, recipes and emergency signs use it, and exactly why it can feel harsh in conversation. English therefore keeps a set of dampers. Adding “just” shrinks the effort (“just press enter”). Adding “try” frames the action as an experiment rather than a command, which also protects you if the advice fails. Moving to an infinitive structure removes you from the sentence entirely (“it’s a good idea to check first”), making the advice sound like a general truth rather than your personal instruction. When you write instructions for someone to follow, use imperatives and be consistent: mixing “open the file” with “you should open the file” makes a list harder to follow. When you advise a person about their own decision, move up the softness scale and let them own the choice.

dynamics.name: Why did you bring that?

dynamics.payoff: Rotating frames stops the class from settling on “to + verb” forever.

At least one warning with “Make sure…” or “Don’t…”.

units.title: SYNC
units.theme: Anchoring events to a moment in time

overview.intro: Two clauses, one clock. This node teaches you to attach a description to a moment (“the year when I left home”) and to line up two events in time (“after I sent it, she called”). These structures are what turn a list of sentences into a narrative a listener can follow.
goals: Define a time expression with a relative clause using when.
Link two events with when, after, before, while, as soon as and until.
Use the correct tense in each clause, especially in future time clauses.
overview.outcome: By the end you can narrate a turning point in your life with several linked clauses, and describe a routine where two things happen in a fixed order.

vocab.def: a very short period of time; a point in time.
vocab.use: “The moment (that)” works as a conjunction meaning “as soon as”: “Call me the moment you arrive.”
examples: I remember the moment when I got the news.
Wait a moment, please.
vocab.colloc: at the moment · in a moment · the moment you arrive

vocab.def: the moment when an important change happens.
vocab.use: Very useful with relative clauses of time: “That was the turning point when everything changed.”
examples: Losing that job was a turning point in my life.
The meeting was a turning point for the company.
vocab.colloc: a major turning point · reach a turning point

vocab.def: immediately after.
vocab.use: Followed by a present tense for the future: “I’ll call you as soon as I get home”, never “as soon as I will get”.
examples: As soon as the file uploads, we can start.
Let me know as soon as you hear anything.
vocab.colloc: as soon as possible · as soon as I can

vocab.def: during the same period as.
vocab.use: For two simultaneous actions, often with a continuous tense: “While I was cooking, she called.”
examples: While you were out, someone left a message.
I listen to podcasts while I drive.
vocab.colloc: while waiting · meanwhile · a while ago

vocab.def: up to the moment when something happens.
vocab.use: Marks an end point, not a duration: “I waited until six”. With a negative it means “not before”: “Don’t leave until I call.”
examples: We stayed until the rain stopped.
I won’t decide until I speak to her.
vocab.colloc: until now · up until then · not until

vocab.def: a length of time with a beginning and an end.
vocab.use: Often followed by “of”: “a period of six months”, “a difficult period in my life”.
examples: That was a strange period of my life.

vocab.colloc: a short period · during that period · a period of change

vocab.def: to finish a course of study and receive a qualification.
vocab.use: “Graduate from + institution”, “graduate in + subject”: “She graduated from university in 2020.”
examples: When I graduated, I had no idea what to do.
He graduated in engineering.
vocab.colloc: graduate from · a recent graduate · graduation day

vocab.def: to understand something suddenly and clearly.
vocab.use: Followed by a that-clause: “I realised that I was wrong.” Not the same as “to make something real”, which is a rarer use.
examples: I only realised the problem when it was too late.
She realised she had forgotten her keys.
vocab.colloc: suddenly realise · didn’t realise · come to realise

vocab.def: at the same time as something else, in a different place.
vocab.use: An adverb, not a conjunction: it connects sentences, not clauses. “Meanwhile, the guests were waiting.”
examples: Meanwhile, nobody had told the client.

vocab.colloc: meanwhile · in the meantime

vocab.def: in the end, after a long time or several problems.

vocab.colloc: eventually happen · eventually gave up

vocab.def: before or at the moment when something else happens.
vocab.use: Followed by a present tense for the future: “By the time you arrive, I’ll have finished.”

vocab.use: Links two moments: “The file is uploading. In the meantime, check your email.”

vocab.colloc: in the meantime · meanwhile

grammar.name: Relative clauses of time with “when”
grammar.short: the day when we met · the year when everything changed
grammar.rule: A relative clause of time defines or describes a time expression. “When” introduces it, and it always refers back to a noun that names a period or a point in time: day, year, moment, summer, time.
form: noun of time + when + subject + verb → I still remember the day when we met.
“When” can often be dropped: the day we met, the year I graduated.
Alternatives: the day (that) we met, the day on which we met (formal).
Non-defining, with a comma: In 2020, when everything closed, I started studying online.
notes: “When” only follows a time noun. For places use “where”, for reasons “why”, for people “who”, for things “that / which”.
In defining clauses “when” is optional and its absence is very common in speech: “Do you remember the night we got lost?”
A comma changes the job of the clause: with no comma it identifies which time you mean; with commas it adds extra information about a time already identified.
Do not repeat the time word inside the clause: “the day when we met on that day” is redundant.
“When” as a relative pronoun is different from “when” as a conjunction of time — the first modifies a noun, the second modifies the whole clause.
grammar.deep: Relative clauses of time solve a specific problem: how to say which moment you mean without starting a new sentence. Compare “I remember a day. We met that day.” with “I remember the day when we met.” The information is identical, but the second version subordinates one idea to the other, and subordination is what makes writing sound adult. The definite article is a good clue that you need one: as soon as you say “the day”, “the year” or “the moment”, your listener expects you to specify which — and a “when” clause is the natural specification. The optional “when” is worth practising deliberately, because dropping it is a fast route to a more natural rhythm: “the summer I turned eighteen” sounds like a story; “the summer when I turned eighteen” sounds like a report. Both are correct, so use the choice for style.

the city where I grew up
the app that tracks my hours

examples: That was the summer when I decided to change careers.
Do you remember the moment we realised the file was gone?
In 2019, when I was still studying, I worked two jobs.
There are days when nothing goes right.
grammar.watch: Use “when” only after a time noun; after a place noun use “where”, not “when”.
more: That was the summer when I decided to change careers.
Do you remember the moment we realised the file was gone?
In 2019, when I was still studying, I worked two jobs.
I’ll never forget the day when the whole system went down.
There are weeks when nothing happens and days when everything does.
The year I graduated was the hardest one.

fix.wrong: the place when we met
fix.right: the place where we met
fix.why: “When” only follows a time noun; places take “where”.

fix.wrong: the day when we met it was raining
fix.right: On the day when we met, it was raining.
fix.why: The relative clause modifies a noun; the main clause still needs its own structure.

fix.wrong: I remember the moment which I understood.
fix.right: I remember the moment when I understood.
fix.why: With a time noun the relative word is “when”, or nothing at all.

drill.name: Name the moment
drill.prompt: Complete each phrase with a relative clause of time, then say the same thing again with “when” dropped.

dialogue.line: When did you decide to move?

rows: the year when I left / the year I left
the client whose order was lost

grammar.sound: When “when” is dropped, the two clauses run together with no pause: “the day we met”. Inserting a pause there sounds like a hesitation, not a clause.

grammar.name: Adverbial clauses of time: when, after, before
grammar.short: After I finish, I’ll call you. / I’ll call when I get home.
grammar.rule: An adverbial clause of time says when the main action happens. It can come first or second in the sentence; if it comes first, it takes a comma. English never uses “will” inside a time clause — the future is carried by the main clause alone.
form: When + subject + verb: When I got home, everyone was asleep.
After / Before + clause: After she left, I locked up. / Before you go, sign this.
Future rule: As soon as I finish, I’ll send it. (present tense in the time clause)
Reduced forms with -ing: After finishing, I went home. / Before leaving, check the lights.
Order is free: I’ll call you when I arrive. / When I arrive, I’ll call you.
notes: This is the rule that decides marks in exams: “When I will arrive” is always wrong. Use the present simple, or the present perfect if you want to stress completion: “as soon as I’ve finished”.
“When” allows the two events to be either simultaneous or sequential; “while” insists they overlap; “as soon as” insists there is no gap between them.
In past narration, “after” and “before” already show the order, so the past perfect is optional: “After I sent it, she called” is as correct as “After I had sent it…”.
A reduced clause with -ing is only possible when both clauses share the same subject: “Before leaving, I locked the door” (I left, I locked).
Punctuation: comma when the time clause opens the sentence, no comma when it closes it.
grammar.deep: Time clauses look easy and then quietly break sentences, because they run on a rule that feels illogical: the clause is about the future, but its verb is in the present. The reason is that English marks the future only once. The main clause carries “will” or “going to”, and once the sentence is anchored in the future, the subordinate clause does not need to repeat it — the conjunction (“when”, “after”, “as soon as”) already tells you where you are. Spanish uses a subjunctive in exactly this slot, which is why the error is so persistent for Spanish speakers: there is a form in your first language, and English seems to leave the slot empty. It does not — it fills it with the present simple. The second thing to master is conjunction choice, because it encodes your interpretation of events: “when the manager arrived, we started” (sequence), “while the manager was arriving, we started” (overlap), “as soon as the manager arrived, we started” (immediate). Same facts, three different stories.

units.title: CONTRAST
units.theme: Then, now, next — and what happens if

overview.intro: This node puts three time frames in the same paragraph so you can talk about change, and then introduces the first conditional: the grammar of consequences. Both structures depend on the same skill — keeping each clause in the tense its job requires.
goals: Contrast past, present and future in one connected description of change.
Build first conditional sentences with if + present simple and will in the main clause.
Use unless, as long as and in case correctly inside conditional sentences.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe how your life or your city has changed across three time frames, and explain the consequences of a real decision.

vocab.def: asking or saying what something was like before.
vocab.use: “What did it use to be like?” is the standard question about a past state. Answer with “used to be + adjective”.
examples: What did your neighbourhood use to be like?
It used to be much quieter.
vocab.colloc: what was it like · it used to be · not like it used to be

vocab.def: in the present, in contrast with the past.
vocab.use: Usually at the beginning or end of the sentence and always with a present tense: “Nowadays everyone works remotely.”
examples: Nowadays most people pay with their phones.
People used to write letters; nowadays they text.
vocab.colloc: nowadays · these days · not nowadays

vocab.def: to believe something will happen.
vocab.use: “Expect + to + verb” or “expect that…”: “I expect to finish by six.” Not the same as “wait for”, which is physical.
examples: I expect prices will keep rising.
We weren’t expecting so many people.
vocab.colloc: expect a change · as expected · better than expected

vocab.def: if not; except if.
vocab.use: Already negative, so the verb after it stays positive: “unless you pay” = “if you don’t pay”. Never “unless you don’t pay”.
examples: Unless we leave now, we’ll miss the train.
I won’t say anything unless she asks.
vocab.colloc: unless you · not unless · unless something changes

vocab.def: only on the condition that.
vocab.use: Followed by a present tense with future meaning: “as long as you tell me first”. Synonym: “provided that” (more formal).
examples: You can borrow it as long as you return it tomorrow.
It’s fine as long as nobody complains.
vocab.colloc: as long as you like · just as long as · so long as

vocab.def: the result of an action, usually a serious one.
vocab.use: “As a consequence of + noun” or “the consequences of + noun”. More neutral synonym: “result”.
examples: There will be consequences if we ignore this.
As a consequence, the project stopped.
vocab.colloc: serious consequences · face the consequences · as a consequence

vocab.def: to get better, or make something better.
vocab.use: Works with and without an object: “My English has improved” and “I want to improve my English”.
examples: Traffic has improved since they opened the new road.
How can we improve the process?
vocab.colloc: improve rapidly · a big improvement · improve on it

vocab.def: a general direction of change over time.
vocab.use: “A trend towards + noun/-ing”: “a trend towards working from home”. Adjective: “trendy” (fashionable) is different.
examples: There’s a clear trend towards online study.
The trend is likely to continue.
vocab.colloc: a growing trend · reverse the trend · current trends

vocab.def: as a precaution, because something might happen.
vocab.use: Never with “will”: “Take an umbrella in case it rains.” Not the same as “if” — it means you act before knowing.
examples: Save the file in case the laptop crashes.
I’ll take cash in case the card doesn’t work.
vocab.colloc: just in case · in case of emergency

vocab.def: slowly, over a period of time.
vocab.use: Common in descriptions of change, usually before the verb: “Things gradually got better.”
examples: The situation gradually improved.
I gradually got used to the schedule.
vocab.colloc: gradually increase · gradually disappear

vocab.def: at that time in the past, in contrast with now.
vocab.use: Sits at the start or end of a past sentence and pairs naturally with “used to”: “Back then we used to write letters.”
examples: Back then nobody had a mobile phone.
We were students back then, so we had no money.
vocab.colloc: back then · way back then · things were different back then

vocab.def: to reach a final situation you did not plan.
vocab.use: Followed by -ing, an adjective or a place: “I ended up working from home.” Inseparable.
examples: We ended up staying an extra week.
If you don’t book now, you’ll end up paying double.
vocab.colloc: end up doing · end up with · end up somewhere

grammar.name: Time contrast: past, present, future
grammar.short: I used to… now I… and next year I’m going to…
grammar.rule: To describe change you need three tenses working in the same paragraph: a past form for what is no longer true, a present form for the current situation, and a future form for what comes next. The connectors mark the shift so your listener follows the movement.
form: Past: used to + verb / simple past → I used to commute two hours a day.
Present: present simple or present continuous → Now I work from home.
Future: be going to / will → Next year I’m going to move closer to the office.
Change connectors: but now, these days, nowadays, at the moment, in the future, from now on, by next year.
notes: Keep the subject and the topic constant while you change the tense; the contrast is only visible if everything else stays the same.
“Now” and “nowadays” pull a present tense; “used to” and “back then” pull a past; “next year” and “soon” pull a future. Let the marker choose the verb.
The present perfect belongs in this paragraph too, as the bridge between past and present: “Things have changed a lot since then.”
Do not mix “used to” with a present marker: “Nowadays I used to work at home” is a contradiction.
In writing, one connector per shift is enough — three “nowadays” in a paragraph sounds mechanical.
grammar.deep: This is less a new structure than a discipline: managing tense across a whole paragraph instead of one sentence. Most learners can produce each form in isolation and then lose control when the frames alternate, because every clause needs its own time anchor. A practical method is to build the paragraph as a table before you speak: column one, what was true; column two, what is true; column three, what will be true. Then say each row with the same subject. Notice that the present perfect is the natural hinge between the first two columns, because its whole job is to link a past event to the present situation — “I used to smoke, I’ve stopped now, and I’m going to run a 10K in June” is a complete story in three tenses. English also expects a visible connector at each shift; without “but now” or “these days”, a listener may hear your present sentence as part of the past narration.

rows: used to / back then / in those days
Things have changed a lot so far.

grammar.sound: “Used to” is said /ˈjuːstə/ with an /s/, not a /z/, and the two words run together. Learners who pronounce /ˈjuːzd tuː/ sound like they mean the verb “to use”.

grammar.name: Conditional sentences with if clauses (first conditional)
grammar.short: If it rains, we’ll cancel.
grammar.rule: The first conditional talks about a real, possible future. The if-clause states the condition in the present simple; the main clause states the consequence with will, going to, an imperative or a modal. As in time clauses, “will” never appears after “if” in this pattern.
form: If + present simple, will + base verb → If you send it today, they’ll reply tomorrow.
Reversed order, no comma: They’ll reply tomorrow if you send it today.
Other main clauses: If you finish early, call me. / If it rains, we might stay home.
Unless = if not → Unless you hurry, you’ll be late.
As long as / provided that = only on this condition → You can come as long as you behave.
notes: “If I will…” is the classic error. The condition takes the present simple: “If I have time, I’ll help you.”
A comma separates the clauses only when the if-clause comes first.
“If” means it may or may not happen; “when” means it certainly will: “If I see her, I’ll tell her” vs “When I see her, I’ll tell her.”
“Unless” is inherently negative, so keep the verb after it positive: “unless you tell me”, not “unless you don’t tell me”.
The zero conditional (if + present, present) is for general truths: “If you heat water to 100°, it boils.” Same shape, different meaning.
grammar.deep: A conditional sentence is a small machine with two slots: the condition and the consequence. English keeps the machine honest by marking the future only once, in the consequence slot, which is why the condition slot takes a present tense even though it points forward. Once you accept that, the first conditional becomes a flexible tool rather than a formula, because you can change the consequence to fit your intention: “will” for a prediction, “going to” for a plan, an imperative for an instruction (“If it breaks, call me”), and a modal for degrees of possibility (“If she asks, I might tell her”). The choice between “if”, “when” and “unless” carries real information about your certainty, and mixing them up will genuinely mislead a listener — “when you finish” tells your colleague you assume the task will be done; “if you finish” quietly suggests you doubt it. Later nodes will move this same machine into the unreal past (node 15); the shape you learn here is the foundation of all of it.

chart.title: First conditional variations
rows: we’re going to start without you.

examples: If I finish the report today, I’ll take tomorrow off.
We won’t get tickets unless we book this week.
If the payment doesn’t arrive, call the bank immediately.
You can use my laptop as long as you don’t install anything.
grammar.watch: No “will” after “if” in a first conditional: “If I have time”, never “If I will have time”.
more: If you leave now, you’ll catch the six o’clock train.
If it rains tomorrow, we’ll move the class online.
They won’t send the invoice unless you confirm the address.
If you need help, call me — I’m at home all evening.
As long as the file is under 10 MB, the system will accept it.
If she doesn’t reply by Friday, I’m going to phone the office.

fix.wrong: If it will rain, we’ll cancel.
fix.right: If it rains, we’ll cancel.
fix.why: The if-clause takes the present simple even though the meaning is future.

fix.wrong: If you won’t hurry, you’ll miss it.
fix.right: If you don’t hurry, you’ll miss it.
fix.why: The negative in the condition is “don’t”, not “won’t”.

fix.wrong: Unless you don’t pay, they’ll cut the service.
fix.right: Unless you pay, they’ll cut the service.
fix.why: “Unless” already means “if not”; a second negative reverses the meaning.

If it rains, we’ll stay in.

as a precaution, before the event

We’ll go even if it rains.

grammar.sound: In fast speech “will” contracts onto the subject — “we’ll”, “they’ll”, “it’ll” /ˈɪtl̩/ — while the if-clause stays unstressed. If both clauses are stressed equally, the sentence sounds like a warning.

speaking.text: Describe your city, your job or your habits across three time frames in one minute. Your partner counts your tense shifts and flags any missing connector.
Start with a condition. Each student turns the previous consequence into a new condition: “If it rains, we’ll stay in. If we stay in, we’ll cook…”
Agree the rules for sharing a flat or a project. Every rule must use if, unless or as long as.

tips: Let the time marker choose the tense, clause by clause.
“If” = maybe; “when” = certainly. Choose deliberately.
After “unless”, keep the verb positive.

quiz.q: If the meeting ___ early, I’ll join you for lunch.
quiz.explain: The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present simple; only the main clause carries the future.

dynamics.name: Then / now gallery
dynamics.how: Students bring or sketch an image of a place they know and pin it up. Everyone circulates and produces three sentences per image: how it used to be, how it is, what will happen next.
dynamics.payoff: Forces the three-frame paragraph out of visual prompts rather than memory.

dynamics.name: Domino conditionals
dynamics.how: Student 1 gives a first conditional. Student 2 must start with the previous result: “If we miss the train, we’ll be late.” → “If we’re late, they’ll start without us.” Six links or the group restarts.
dynamics.payoff: Repeated production with automatic error detection — a broken chain is audible.

dynamics.name: Life audit
dynamics.how: Each student interviews their partner about five areas of life (work, home, health, money, study) and takes notes in three columns: then, now, next. Then reports two of them to another pair.
dynamics.payoff: The note-taking grid enforces the tense contrast before speaking.

dynamics.name: Unless court
dynamics.how: Teacher reads a sentence with “if not”; students race to rewrite it with “unless” on mini-whiteboards. Any double negative loses the point.
dynamics.payoff: Kills the “unless … don’t” error in one short burst.

writing.title: How my city changed
writing.brief: Describe how a place you know has changed. Write one paragraph in three frames (used to / now / going to) and a second paragraph of three first conditionals predicting what will happen if the change continues.
criteria: Three clearly marked time frames in paragraph one.
Three first conditionals in paragraph two, none with “will” after “if”.
At least one sentence with unless or as long as.

homework.title: Then, now, next
homework.task: Write six sentences about your own life using used to, now and going to (two of each), then six first conditionals about your next month. Underline the verb after every “if” and check that none of them is “will”.

test.q: There ___ a cinema here, but it closed in 2018.
test.explain: The past habit form is “used to” + base verb.

test.q: If you ___ me the file today, I’ll read it tonight.
test.explain: The if-clause takes the present simple.

test.q: ___ everyone shops online.
test.explain: A present-tense sentence needs a present marker.

test.q: We’ll start at nine ___ everybody arrives on time.
test.explain: “As long as” states the condition that must be true.

test.q: They won’t come ___ you invite them personally.
test.explain: “Unless” means “if not”, which fits the negative main clause.

board: Three panels across the board: THEN | NOW | NEXT, each with its own tense written under the heading.
Under THEN: used to + base · simple past · back then, in those days.
Under NOW: present simple / continuous · nowadays, these days, at the moment.
Under NEXT: going to · will · next year, soon, by 2030.
