units.title: PREFERENCE
units.theme: Likes, dislikes and the reasons behind them

overview.intro: What you enjoy, what you can’t stand, and why. This node combines gerunds after verbs of liking with the short responses that keep a conversation alive, and then gives you the machinery for stating reasons with “because” and its relatives.
goals: Use gerunds after like, love, enjoy, hate, don’t mind and can’t stand.
Agree and disagree with short responses: so do I, neither do I, I do, I don’t.
Give reasons with because, because of, since and so.
overview.outcome: By the end you can hold a five-turn conversation about preferences, reacting to your partner instead of just listing your own tastes.

vocab.def: to get pleasure from something.
vocab.use: Always followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “I enjoy cooking”, not “I enjoy to cook”. It also needs an object: “Did you enjoy it?”
examples: I really enjoy working with this team.
She enjoyed the concert.
vocab.colloc: enjoy yourself · thoroughly enjoy · enjoy doing something

vocab.def: to hate something intensely.
vocab.use: “Can’t stand + -ing” or a noun: “I can’t stand waiting in queues.” Stronger than “don’t like”.
examples: I can’t stand being interrupted.
He can’t stand the heat.
vocab.colloc: can’t stand it · really can’t stand · can’t stand doing

vocab.def: to be fine with something; to have no objection.
vocab.use: “I don’t mind + -ing”: “I don’t mind working late.” Positive “I mind” is rare; use “it bothers me”.
examples: I don’t mind cooking if someone else cleans.
Do you mind if I sit here?
vocab.colloc: I don’t mind at all · never mind · would you mind

vocab.def: to be very interested in something (informal).
vocab.use: “Be into + noun / -ing”: “I’m into climbing.” Informal but extremely common in spoken English.
examples: She’s really into photography.
I’m not into video games.
vocab.colloc: really into · not into it · what are you into

vocab.def: to like one thing more than another.
vocab.use: Two patterns: “prefer + -ing to + -ing” (I prefer walking to driving) and “prefer + to + verb” (I prefer to walk).
examples: I prefer working mornings to working nights.
Would you prefer to meet on Friday?
vocab.colloc: prefer not to · a personal preference · prefer A to B

vocab.def: not one and not the other.
vocab.use: In short responses it needs inversion: “Neither do I”, “Neither am I”. It carries the negative, so the verb stays positive.
examples: I don’t like horror films. — Neither do I.
Neither of them answered.
vocab.colloc: neither do I · neither of us · me neither

vocab.def: the explanation for something.
vocab.use: “The reason for + noun” or “the reason why + clause”: “the reason for the delay”, “the reason why I left”.
examples: The main reason is the price.
There’s no reason to worry.
vocab.colloc: the main reason · for that reason · no reason at all

vocab.def: used before a noun to give the cause.
vocab.use: “Because of + noun”, “because + full clause”. “Because of the rain” vs “because it rained”.
examples: We cancelled because of the weather.
She left early because of a family problem.
vocab.colloc: because of you · mainly because of · because of that

vocab.def: “boring” describes the thing; “bored” describes the person.
vocab.use: The -ing/-ed pair covers many feelings: interesting/interested, tiring/tired, confusing/confused. Full treatment at node 13.
examples: The film was boring, so I got bored.
I’m bored of doing the same thing.
vocab.colloc: deadly boring · get bored · bored to death

vocab.def: good enough to justify the effort or cost.
vocab.use: “It’s worth + -ing” or “it’s worth it”: “The extra hour was worth it.”
examples: The course was expensive, but it was worth it.
It’s worth trying at least once.
vocab.colloc: well worth it · not worth it · worth every penny

vocab.def: tired of something that has been annoying you for a while.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “I’m fed up with waiting.” Stronger and more personal than “tired of”.
examples: I’m fed up with the noise from upstairs.
She got fed up with explaining the same thing.
vocab.colloc: fed up with · get fed up · absolutely fed up

grammar.name: Gerunds and short responses
grammar.short: I love cooking. — So do I. / I don’t.
grammar.rule: Verbs of liking and disliking are followed by the gerund (-ing) when the object is an activity. In conversation, agreement and disagreement are expressed with a short response that repeats only the auxiliary — never the whole sentence.
form: Verb + -ing: like, love, enjoy, hate, don’t mind, can’t stand, prefer → I hate waiting.
Agreeing with a positive: So do I. / Me too. / So am I. / So did we.
Agreeing with a negative: Neither do I. / Me neither. / Neither am I.
Disagreeing with a positive: I don’t. / Oh, I do. / Really? I don’t.
Disagreeing with a negative: I do. / Oh, I do.
notes: “So” and “neither” both require inversion: “So do I”, “Neither have I” — never “So I do”.
The auxiliary in the response must match the original sentence: “I’m tired” → “So am I”; “I went” → “So did I”; “I’ve finished” → “So have I”.
“Me too” and “me neither” are informal but perfectly acceptable in speech; they never change form.
“Like + to + verb” is also correct and slightly more about habit or choice: “I like to get up early” (my policy) vs “I like getting up early” (I enjoy it).
“Would like” is different from “like”: it means “want” and always takes an infinitive — “I’d like to order”.
grammar.deep: There are two skills here and the second one is what makes you sound like a participant rather than a speaker of prepared sentences. The gerund rule itself is mechanical: after a verb of liking, the activity becomes a noun, so it takes -ing. The response system is more interesting because it is built on echo. English hates repetition, so instead of “I also love cooking”, the language echoes only the grammatical skeleton of what the other person said — the auxiliary — and lets that stand for the whole idea. This means you must listen to the auxiliary, not the content: if your partner said “I’ve never been to Brazil”, your agreement is “Neither have I”, because their sentence was built on “have”. Get into the habit of scanning for the auxiliary while your partner is still speaking, and remember that when a sentence has no auxiliary, the response borrows “do”: “I like it” → “So do I”. The polarity flip is the last piece: “neither” and “me neither” answer a negative, so they need no second negative of their own.
examples: I can’t stand working late. — Neither can I.
I really enjoy travelling on my own. — Do you? I don’t.
I don’t mind driving at night. — So do I… sorry: neither do I.
I’ve never tried it. — Neither have I.
grammar.watch: Match the auxiliary and invert it: “So have I”, “Neither did I”. Never “So I have”.
more: I love working outdoors, but I can’t stand commuting.
She doesn’t mind cooking as long as somebody else washes up.
I enjoy reading before bed. — So do I.
I hate queuing. — Neither do I. It drives me mad.
We really enjoyed meeting your team.
I don’t like driving at night. — I do, actually. The roads are empty.

fix.wrong: I enjoy to cook.
fix.right: I enjoy cooking.
fix.why: Enjoy, can’t stand, don’t mind and finish always take the gerund.

fix.wrong: I love swimming. — So I do.
fix.right: I love swimming. — So do I.
fix.why: Short responses invert the auxiliary: “So do I”, not “So I do”.

fix.wrong: I can’t stand waiting. — So do I.
fix.right: I can’t stand waiting. — Neither can I.
fix.why: A negative statement takes “neither”, and the auxiliary must match (“can”).

drill.name: Match the auxiliary
drill.prompt: Respond to each statement with the correct short response, then add one reason with “because”.

dialogue.line: I really enjoy working from home.
So do I, but I miss the office coffee.
I don’t. I got fed up with the noise there.
Neither did I like it, honestly — I just prefer having people around.

grammar.sound: The short response carries falling stress on the auxiliary and the pronoun: “So DO I”. Flat intonation there sounds sarcastic in English, which is not usually the intention.

grammar.name: Clauses with “because”
grammar.short: I left because I was tired. / because of the traffic.
grammar.rule: “Because” introduces a full clause with its own subject and verb and answers the question “why?”. “Because of” is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or a gerund. Related connectors change the emphasis or the position of the reason.
form: because + subject + verb → I stayed home because I felt ill.
because of + noun/-ing → I stayed home because of the rain.
since / as + clause (reason known, often first) → Since it was raining, we stayed in.
so + result → It was raining, so we stayed in.
the reason why / the reason for → The reason why I called is simple.
notes: “Because” cannot start a sentence in careful written English on its own; it needs a main clause somewhere: “Because I was tired, I left” is fine, but “Because I was tired.” alone is a fragment.
“Because of” must be followed by a noun phrase: “because of the delay”, not “because of the train was late”.
“So” introduces the consequence, “because” the cause — they are mirror images: “I was tired, so I left” = “I left because I was tired”.
“Since” and “as” present the reason as already known or obvious, and usually come first in the sentence; “because” often carries the new or important information and comes second.
Do not use “for” to mean “because” at this level — it is literary and easily misused.
grammar.deep: Cause and consequence are two views of the same relationship, and choosing which one to put in the main clause changes what your listener treats as important. English readers weight the second clause more heavily, so “The flight was cancelled, so we stayed another night” foregrounds the outcome, while “We stayed another night because the flight was cancelled” foregrounds the explanation. Use that deliberately in writing. The grammatical trap is purely mechanical: “because” takes a clause, “because of” takes a noun, and the fastest test is to look at what comes next — if you can see a verb with its own subject, drop the “of”. Watch out for one more thing: over-using “because” makes speech sound like a child explaining. Rotating in “since”, “as”, “so” and “that’s why” gives your reasoning texture, and “the reason why … is that …” is a useful frame when you need to announce that an explanation is coming.

chart.title: Cause and result connectors
rows: I left because I was tired.
I left because of the noise.
I was tired, so I left.
I was tired. That’s why I left.
The reason why I left is that I was tired.

examples: We changed the date because of a scheduling conflict.
Since nobody replied, I made the decision myself.
The train was delayed, so I missed the first session.
The reason why I prefer mornings is that the office is quiet.
grammar.watch: “Because of” + noun, “because” + clause. “Because of it was late” is always wrong.
more: I took the train because the roads were closed.
We cancelled the trip because of the storm.
It was raining, so we stayed in.
Since you’re already here, could you help me for a second?
She left early because of a family emergency.
The shop closed because nobody came in the winter.

fix.wrong: because of it was late
fix.right: because it was late
fix.why: “Because of” takes a noun; a clause with a verb needs plain “because”.

fix.wrong: Because the traffic. I was late.
fix.right: Because of the traffic, I was late.
fix.why: A noun after “because” needs “of”, and the fragment must join the main clause.

fix.wrong: It was raining, because we stayed in.
fix.right: It was raining, so we stayed in.
fix.why: “Because” introduces the cause; the result takes “so”.

drill.name: Three ways to say why
drill.prompt: Take each cause-and-result pair and express it three times: with because, with because of, and with so.

dialogue.line: Why didn’t you come on Saturday?
Because of the weather. The road was flooded.
You could have called.
There was no signal, so I sent a message when I got home.

contrast.title: Cause and result words
rows: It was late, so we stopped.

grammar.sound: “Because” is reduced to /kəz/ or “’cause” in speech, with the stress falling on the reason that follows it, not on the conjunction itself.

speaking.text: Make a statement about something you like or hate. Your partner must respond with a short response (so/neither/I do/I don’t) and add a reason with because. Ten turns without breaking the chain.
In groups, rank five ways of spending a free Sunday. Every argument must contain a gerund and a reason.
Give a statement with “because”. Your partner rewrites it with “because of”, then with “so”, keeping the meaning.

tips: After like, love, hate, enjoy, don’t mind and can’t stand, use -ing.
Listen for the auxiliary — it is what your short response repeats.
“Because of” needs a noun; if you can see a verb, drop the “of”.

quiz.q: I can’t stand ___ in traffic. — Neither ___ I.
quiz.explain: “Can’t stand” takes the gerund, and the short response repeats the same auxiliary — “can” — after “neither”.

dynamics.name: Preference ladder
dynamics.how: Each group ranks eight activities from “love” to “can’t stand”. Every placement must be justified with a gerund and a reason, and the group must reach one agreed order.
dynamics.payoff: Negotiation forces repeated gerunds and real disagreement, not polite listing.

dynamics.name: Mirror match
dynamics.how: Student A makes a statement; B must answer with a short response within three seconds. Any hesitation or wrong auxiliary passes the turn. Ten statements each.
dynamics.payoff: Speed is what turns short responses from a rule into a reflex.

dynamics.name: Find someone who doesn’t
dynamics.how: Students circulate looking for one person who agrees and one who disagrees with each of their five statements, recording the exact response used.
dynamics.payoff: Guarantees both “so/neither” and “I do/I don’t” get produced.

dynamics.name: Because / because of relay
dynamics.how: Teacher calls a cause as a noun or a clause; the first team to shout the correctly matched connector scores. Wrong connector loses the point.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the single most common error in this node.

writing.title: What I love and what I can’t stand
writing.brief: Write about three things you love doing and two you can’t stand. Each one needs a gerund and a reason. Finish with a paragraph about a preference you share with someone, using at least two short responses in reported dialogue.
criteria: Five gerunds after verbs of liking or disliking.
Reasons expressed with because, because of and so at least once each.
Two correctly formed short responses.

homework.title: Agree and disagree
homework.task: Write ten statements about your tastes. Beside each, write how a person who agrees would respond and how a person who disagrees would respond. Check that the auxiliary in the response matches the verb in the statement.

test.q: I can’t stand ___ in queues.
test.explain: “Can’t stand” is followed by the gerund.

test.q: I’ve never been to Japan. — ___ I.
test.explain: A negative statement in the present perfect takes “Neither have I”.

test.q: We stayed at home ___ the storm.
test.explain: “The storm” is a noun, so it needs “because of”.

test.q: I don’t like early mornings. — ___ , actually. I love them.
test.explain: Disagreeing with a negative takes the positive auxiliary alone.

test.q: The train was cancelled, ___ we drove.
test.explain: The second clause is the result, which takes “so”.

board: Left column headed VERB + -ING: like, love, enjoy, hate, don’t mind, can’t stand, prefer.
Right column headed SHORT RESPONSES, split into agree / disagree rows for do, am, have, did, can.
A red arrow marking the inversion: So DO I ✔ · So I do ✘.
Bottom strip: BECAUSE + clause | BECAUSE OF + noun | SO + result.
Corner box: the sentence “because of it was late” with “of” crossed out.

units.title: BLACK BOX
units.theme: When the action matters more than the actor

overview.intro: Sometimes the interesting part of a sentence is not who did it. The passive voice moves the object into the subject position and pushes the agent to the end — or deletes it entirely. This node covers the past passive with “by” and the present passive without it.
goals: Form the passive with be + past participle in the simple past and simple present.
Decide when to include “by + agent” and when to leave it out.
Convert active sentences into passive ones without losing meaning.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe a process, a rule and a historical event in the passive, and explain why the passive was the right choice.

vocab.def: constructed by someone.
vocab.use: “Build – built – built”. The passive is extremely common with buildings and dates: “It was built in 1890.”
examples: The bridge was built two years ago.
Those flats are being built now.
vocab.colloc: was built in · newly built · purpose-built

vocab.def: to create something that did not exist before.
vocab.use: Classic passive verb with “by”: “The telephone was invented by Bell.” Noun: invention; person: inventor.
examples: Penicillin was discovered, not invented.
Who invented this system?
vocab.colloc: invent a machine · a new invention · newly invented

vocab.def: to make or grow something, usually in quantity.
vocab.use: Standard in present passive descriptions: “Coffee is produced in Huila.” Noun: production, produce (food).
examples: Most of our coffee is produced locally.
The factory produces 2,000 units a day.
vocab.colloc: mass-produced · locally produced · production line

vocab.def: to take goods to a place.
vocab.use: Very frequent in the passive: “Your order will be delivered tomorrow.” Noun: delivery.
examples: Packages are delivered every morning.
It was delivered to the wrong address.
vocab.colloc: free delivery · deliver on time · be delivered

vocab.def: to harm something physically.
vocab.use: Passive with no agent is normal when the cause is unknown: “The screen was damaged in transit.”
examples: Two houses were damaged by the storm.
Nothing was damaged, luckily.
vocab.colloc: badly damaged · cause damage · damage control

vocab.def: to permit.
vocab.use: The passive is the standard way to state rules: “Smoking is not allowed here.” Compare “permitted” (more formal).
examples: Photos aren’t allowed inside the museum.
Are we allowed to park here?
vocab.colloc: not allowed · allowed to enter · allow access

vocab.def: the person or thing that performs the action.
vocab.use: In a passive sentence the agent appears after “by”, if it appears at all: “written by a student”.
examples: The agent is usually left out when it’s obvious.
This was signed by the director.
vocab.colloc: by + agent · the agent is unknown

vocab.def: to need officially.
vocab.use: Very common in passive rules: “A visa is required.” “Applicants are required to submit…”.
examples: Proof of address is required.
You’re required to sign here.
vocab.colloc: required by law · a requirement · as required

vocab.def: to deal with something or someone.
vocab.use: “Complaints are handled by the front desk.” Also physical: “Handle with care.”
examples: All requests are handled within 48 hours.
She handled the situation very well.
vocab.colloc: handle a complaint · handle with care · easy to handle

vocab.def: to use something as a foundation.
vocab.use: Fixed preposition: “based on a true story”, “based in Bogotá” (location). Do not mix “on” and “in”.
examples: The film is based on a real case.
Our team is based in Medellín.
vocab.colloc: based on evidence · based in · widely based

vocab.def: to do or complete a piece of planned work.
vocab.use: Very common in the passive: “The tests were carried out last week.” Separable but usually kept together.
examples: The survey was carried out by an independent team.
They carried out repairs overnight.
vocab.colloc: carry out a study · carry out repairs · carried out by

vocab.def: in the beginning, before any change.
vocab.use: Sits before the verb or at the start of the sentence and pairs naturally with the past passive: “It was originally built as a hospital.”
examples: The building was originally a train station.
Originally, the meeting was scheduled for Monday.
vocab.colloc: originally built · originally from · originally planned

grammar.name: Passive with “by” (simple past)
grammar.short: The report was written by an intern.
grammar.rule: The past passive is formed with was / were plus the past participle. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject, and the original subject — the agent — moves to the end after “by”, but only when the agent is worth mentioning.
form: Active: An intern wrote the report. → Passive: The report was written by an intern.
Affirmative: subject + was/were + past participle → The letters were sent yesterday.
Negative: wasn’t / weren’t + participle → It wasn’t signed by the manager.
Question: Was / Were + subject + participle? → Was the file deleted?
Wh-question: When was it published? / Who was it written by?
notes: Only verbs with an object can go into the passive. “Happen”, “arrive”, “go” and “die” have no passive form.
The tense lives in “be”, not in the participle: “was written” (past), “is written” (present), “will be written” (future).
Include “by + agent” only when the agent is new, surprising or important: “The bridge was designed by a local architect.” Otherwise drop it.
Irregular participles must be accurate — the passive exposes them: taken, written, built, sent, made, broken, done.
Keep the participle, not the past form: “was chose” is wrong; it is “was chosen”.
grammar.deep: The passive is a spotlight, not a politeness device. Every sentence has a topic — the thing the sentence is about — and English puts that topic in the subject position. When the interesting thing is the object of the action, the passive lets you keep it at the front: in a paragraph about a building, “It was designed in 1912” keeps the building as the subject and preserves the flow. That is why the passive dominates reports, news and academic writing, and why translating everything into the active often makes a text choppier, not clearer. The one rule to internalise is that the tense is carried entirely by “be”. Learners who write “was wrote” have simply chosen the wrong second element; the past is already in “was”, so the second slot must be the participle. And the agent question is genuinely stylistic: leave out “by” when the agent is unknown, irrelevant or obvious (“the shop was robbed”, “taxes are collected annually”), and keep it when your reader would ask who.

chart.title: Active → past passive
rows: The telephone was invented by Bell.
This was written by a student.
Two houses were damaged by the storm.

examples: The system was updated last night, so some settings were reset.
This photograph was taken by my grandfather in 1968.
Were you invited to the launch?
Nothing was decided at the meeting.
grammar.watch: After was/were, use the past participle, not the past simple: “was taken”, never “was took”.
more: The bridge was built by a Colombian engineer in 1932.
These photographs were taken by my grandmother.
The decision wasn’t made by the committee; it came from the director.
Were the invitations sent by email or by post?
The report was written by two interns and reviewed by the manager.
Our office was designed by a studio in Medellín.

fix.wrong: The report was write by an intern.
fix.right: The report was written by an intern.
fix.why: The passive needs the past participle, not the base form.

fix.wrong: The letters was sent yesterday.
fix.right: The letters were sent yesterday.
fix.why: “Be” agrees with the new subject, which is plural here.

fix.wrong: The song was composed from Mozart.
fix.right: The song was composed by Mozart.
fix.why: The agent takes “by”; “from” marks material or origin.

drill.name: Flip the sentence
drill.prompt: Turn each active sentence into a passive one, keeping the agent with “by”. Then say it again without the agent and decide which version is better.
items: A local artist painted the mural.
Someone stole my bike last night.
The team finished the prototype in March.

dialogue.line: Who made this?
It was made by a workshop in Popayán, apparently.
And the design?
The design was originally drawn by the owner’s father. Nothing has been changed since.

grammar.sound: “Was” and “were” are unstressed and reduced to /wəz/ and /wə/; the stress lands on the participle. “The report was WRITten” — stressing “was” makes it sound like a correction.

grammar.name: Passive without “by” (simple present)
grammar.short: Coffee is grown here. Smoking isn’t allowed.
grammar.rule: The present passive is formed with am / is / are plus the past participle. It is the normal way to describe processes, rules and general facts, and in most of these sentences the agent is deliberately omitted because it is unknown, obvious or unimportant.
form: Affirmative: subject + am/is/are + past participle → Tickets are checked at the door.
Negative: isn’t / aren’t + participle → Dogs aren’t allowed inside.
Question: Is / Are + subject + participle? → Is breakfast included?
With modals: must be signed, can be found, should be kept.
Process sequence: First the beans are picked, then they are dried and sorted.
notes: Rules and notices live in this structure: “Payment is required in advance”, “Helmets must be worn”.
In process descriptions, the agent is almost never mentioned — the sequence is the point, not the workers.
The subject and “be” must agree: “The documents are checked”, “The document is checked”.
Adverbs of frequency go between “be” and the participle: “Files are usually backed up at midnight.”
“Born” only exists in the passive: “I was born in 1998” — never “I borned”.
grammar.deep: Present passives are the grammar of institutions. Signs, terms and conditions, manuals and procedure documents all use them because they describe what happens regardless of who does it, and because the anonymity is functional rather than evasive: nobody cares which member of staff checks the tickets. This is also why the passive is so useful when you describe a process — each step keeps the product as its subject, so the reader follows one thing through a chain of actions rather than tracking a cast of people. Two practical habits will improve your writing quickly. First, when you catch yourself writing a vague active subject — “they check the tickets”, “people say that” — consider a passive instead: “tickets are checked”, “it is said that”. Second, do not overshoot: if the actor is genuinely the point, the active is stronger and shorter. The passive earns its place when the actor is noise.

chart.title: When to omit the agent
rows: The mural was painted by students.

examples: The beans are picked by hand, washed, and then dried in the sun.
Mobile phones aren’t allowed during the exam.
Is service included in the price?
Applications are reviewed within ten working days.
grammar.watch: “Born” has no active form: “I was born in Cali”, never “I born” or “I have born”.
more: Coffee is grown in the mountains around here.
Tickets are checked at the entrance.
Dogs aren’t allowed in the reading room.
How is this word pronounced?
These containers are made from recycled plastic.
The results are published every Friday morning.

fix.wrong: Smoking not allowed here.
fix.right: Smoking isn’t allowed here.
fix.why: The passive always needs a form of “be”, even in a notice.

fix.wrong: This bags are made of paper.
fix.right: These bags are made of paper.
fix.why: Agreement error carried into the passive; the plural subject needs “these … are”.

fix.wrong: English speaks in many countries.
fix.right: English is spoken in many countries.
fix.why: The subject receives the action, so the verb must be passive.

drill.name: How it’s done
drill.prompt: Describe each process in three present passive sentences, in order, with no named agent.

dialogue.line: Is the water here treated?
Yes, it’s filtered twice before it’s distributed.
And is it tested regularly?
Samples are taken every day. The results are published online.

grammar.sound: “Is” contracts onto the subject in speech (“it’s grown”, “that’s made”), which makes the passive easy to miss when listening. Train the ear on the participle, not the auxiliary.

speaking.text: Explain how something is made or done — coffee, a passport, a delivery — in six present-passive steps, with no agents.
In pairs, write the eight rules of a gym, a library or a shared flat using present passives with allowed, required, permitted and must be.
Describe five objects or buildings in your city in the past passive. Include “by” only where the agent genuinely matters.

tips: The tense sits in “be”; the second word is always a participle.
Drop “by” unless your reader would ask who did it.
Learn irregular participles in threes — the passive puts them on display.

quiz.q: This building ___ in 1904 by a Belgian architect.
quiz.explain: A finished past event with a named agent takes was + past participle: “was designed by…”.

dynamics.name: Museum labels
dynamics.how: Each pair writes four museum labels for objects in the room or in photos: what it is, when it was made, who it was made by, what it is used for. Labels are posted and read aloud.
dynamics.payoff: Produces both passives in a genre that genuinely requires them.

dynamics.name: Whodunnit
dynamics.how: Groups get a crime-scene list of five facts in the passive with no agent (“The window was broken…”). They must reconstruct the story, then present it, adding agents where they can prove them.
dynamics.payoff: Shows exactly why the agent is dropped and when it comes back.

dynamics.name: Process race
dynamics.how: Each team is given a product and has four minutes to write the six stages of how it is made, all in the present passive. Points for correct passives, not for accuracy of the process.
dynamics.payoff: High volume of present passives under time pressure.

dynamics.name: Notice board
dynamics.how: Students rewrite five active classroom rules as passive notices (“You must not eat here” → “Eating is not allowed”). The best five are posted on the wall for the rest of the unit.
dynamics.payoff: Links the structure to real signs students see every day.

writing.title: How it is made
writing.brief: Choose a product or a dish from your region. Write one paragraph describing how it is made, in the present passive with no agents, and one paragraph about its history in the past passive, naming at least two agents with “by”.
criteria: Five present passives with no agent.
Three past passives, two of them with “by”.
Correct past participles throughout.

homework.title: Active into passive
homework.task: Rewrite ten active sentences from a news article as passives, then decide for each whether the agent is worth keeping. Write one line explaining each decision.

test.q: The mural ___ by a local artist in 2019.
test.explain: A finished past action with a named agent takes was + past participle.

test.q: Coffee ___ in this region.
test.explain: A general present process takes the present passive.

test.q: Dogs ___ in the library.
test.explain: The plural subject takes “aren’t” plus the past participle.

test.q: These bags are made ___ recycled plastic.
test.explain: Material that has been transformed takes “from”; the agent would take “by”.

test.q: ___ the invitations sent by email?
test.explain: A plural subject in a past passive question takes “were”.

units.title: TRACE
units.theme: Background action, interrupted action, and effort still in progress

overview.intro: Two continuous tenses with two very different jobs. The past continuous paints the background of a story and gets interrupted by the simple past. The present perfect continuous measures an activity that started in the past and is still running, or has only just stopped.
goals: Contrast the past continuous and the simple past in narration.
Form the present perfect continuous and use it with for, since, all day and lately.
Choose between the present perfect simple and continuous according to focus.
overview.outcome: By the end you can narrate an incident with background and interruption, and explain what you have been working on recently.

vocab.def: to stop someone or something in the middle of an action.
vocab.use: Transitive: “Sorry to interrupt you.” Noun: interruption. The past continuous is the tense that gets interrupted.
examples: He interrupted me while I was speaking.
Sorry to interrupt, but there’s a call for you.
vocab.colloc: constantly interrupt · sorry to interrupt · without interruption

vocab.def: in the recent past, in a period still open.
vocab.use: Both signal the present perfect (simple or continuous): “I’ve been sleeping badly lately.”
examples: Have you seen him lately?
I’ve been travelling a lot recently.
vocab.colloc: lately · until recently · just recently

vocab.def: for the whole of that period.
vocab.use: Strong triggers for the present perfect continuous: “I’ve been working all day.”
examples: It’s been raining all day.
I’ve been on calls all morning.
vocab.colloc: all day long · all week · all this time

vocab.def: to investigate something.
vocab.use: Inseparable. Frequently in the continuous: “We’ve been looking into the problem.”
examples: I’ll look into it this afternoon.
They’ve been looking into the cause for weeks.
vocab.colloc: look into a matter · worth looking into

vocab.def: movement towards a goal.
vocab.use: Noncount: “a lot of progress”, never “progresses”. “Make progress”, not “do progress”.
examples: We’ve been making good progress.
There’s been little progress so far.
vocab.colloc: make progress · slow progress · work in progress

vocab.def: to handle a problem or a person.
vocab.use: Inseparable: “deal with it”. Past: dealt (pronounced “delt”).
examples: I’ve been dealing with complaints all week.
Who deals with invoices here?
vocab.colloc: deal with a problem · hard to deal with

vocab.def: extremely tired.
vocab.use: A strong adjective, so no “very”: use “absolutely exhausted”. Often the result of a continuous activity.
examples: I’m exhausted — I’ve been driving since six.
She looked exhausted after the shift.
vocab.colloc: absolutely exhausted · mentally exhausted

vocab.def: to watch something carefully over time.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase with “on”: “Keep an eye on the server.” Often paired with continuous tenses.
examples: We’ve been keeping an eye on the numbers.
Can you keep an eye on my bag?
vocab.colloc: keep an eye on it · keep a close eye on

vocab.def: to continue; to happen.
vocab.use: “How long has this been going on?” is the classic present perfect continuous question.
examples: What’s going on here?
This has been going on for months.
vocab.colloc: go on for hours · what’s going on · go on doing

vocab.def: markers of the interrupting event in a story.
vocab.use: They introduce the simple past that breaks into a past continuous: “I was leaving when suddenly the alarm went off.”
examples: Just then, the lights went out.
Suddenly everyone started shouting.
vocab.colloc: suddenly stop · just then · all of a sudden

vocab.def: to meet someone by chance, or to hit a problem unexpectedly.
vocab.use: Inseparable, and very common in narration: “I ran into an old colleague while I was waiting.”
examples: I ran into Ana while I was leaving the office.
We ran into a few problems during the migration.
vocab.colloc: run into someone · run into trouble · run into difficulties

vocab.def: during the recent period up to now.
vocab.use: Goes at the end or beginning of the sentence and pulls a perfect tense: “I’ve been sleeping badly lately.”
examples: Have you been working a lot lately?
Lately I’ve been cycling to work.
vocab.colloc: lately · not lately · what have you been up to lately?

grammar.name: Past continuous vs simple past
grammar.short: I was cooking when the phone rang.
grammar.rule: The past continuous (was/were + -ing) describes an action in progress at a past moment: the background. The simple past describes a completed action: the event. In a narrative, the simple past interrupts the past continuous.
form: Past continuous: was / were + -ing → At eight I was still working.
Interruption pattern: past continuous + when + simple past → I was leaving when he called.
Parallel actions: while + past continuous, past continuous → While I was cooking, she was studying.
Negative / question: I wasn’t listening. / What were you doing at ten?
notes: “When” usually introduces the short, completed action; “while” usually introduces the longer, background one. That is why “I was reading when the light went out” and “While I was reading, the light went out” both work.
The past continuous sets scenes and moods in storytelling: “It was raining and nobody was talking.”
State verbs resist the continuous: know, believe, own, belong, want. Say “I knew”, not “I was knowing”.
Two past continuous clauses joined by “while” mean the actions overlapped completely.
The past continuous can also express an interrupted plan: “I was going to call you, but I fell asleep.”
grammar.deep: Narration in English is built on two layers, and the tenses keep them apart. The past continuous is the canvas — weather, feelings, activities already under way — and the simple past is the paint: the events that actually move the story forward. If you tell a story entirely in the simple past, everything sounds equally important; if you tell it entirely in the past continuous, nothing ever happens. Practise combining them in one sentence with “when”: background first, then the event. There is a subtlety worth noticing in the interrupted-plan use: “I was walking to the station when I saw her” tells you the walk was interrupted, not necessarily abandoned, while “I walked to the station and saw her” makes both events complete and sequential. Choosing the continuous is therefore a way of signalling that the action was in progress and possibly incomplete — a small tense choice carrying real narrative information.

chart.title: Background vs event
rows: I was sleeping when the alarm rang.
While I was sleeping, the alarm rang.
She was cooking while I was working.
I woke up, showered and left.
It was raining and the streets were empty.

examples: I was crossing the street when a car came round the corner.
While we were waiting for the bus, it started to rain.
What were you doing when the power went out?
She wasn’t paying attention, so she missed the announcement.
grammar.watch: Do not use the continuous with state verbs: “I was knowing him” is wrong — say “I knew him”.
more: I was reading on the sofa when the doorbell rang.
While she was presenting, the projector died.
They were arguing about the budget when the director walked in.
What were you doing at eleven last night?
We were driving home when we ran into the storm.
He wasn’t listening, so he missed the question.

fix.wrong: I was cooking when the phone was ringing.
fix.right: I was cooking when the phone rang.
fix.why: The interruption is a completed event and takes the simple past.

fix.wrong: While I studied, my brother was calling me twice.
fix.right: While I was studying, my brother called me twice.
fix.why: The long background action is continuous; the short repeated event is simple.

fix.wrong: I was knowing the answer.
fix.right: I knew the answer.
fix.why: State verbs like know, believe and belong do not take the continuous.

drill.name: Interrupted
drill.prompt: Complete each background with an interruption in the simple past, then swap the order and add a comma.
items: She was writing the report when…
They were boarding the plane when…
I was about to leave when…

dialogue.line: How did the accident happen?
I was turning into the car park when another car came out fast.
Was anyone hurt?
No. We were both driving slowly, so it was only the mirror.

contrast.title: Which past tense?
rows: It was raining and nobody was talking.
the event that moves the story
While I was cooking, she was working.
We used to meet on Fridays.

grammar.sound: “Was” and “were” reduce to /wəz/ and /wə/, and “-ing” often loses the /g/ in casual speech. The information is in the main verb: “I was WORking when he CALLED.”

grammar.name: Present perfect continuous
grammar.short: I’ve been waiting for an hour.
grammar.rule: The present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing) links an activity to the present through its duration. It says how long something has been going on — either it is still happening, or it stopped so recently that the effects are visible.
form: Affirmative: subject + have/has been + -ing → She’s been studying since eight.
Negative: haven’t / hasn’t been + -ing → I haven’t been sleeping well.
Question: Have you been waiting long? / How long has this been going on?
Duration markers: for two hours, since Monday, all day, lately, recently.
notes: Use it for duration and activity; use the present perfect simple for completion and quantity: “I’ve been writing emails” (activity) vs “I’ve written six emails” (result).
Visible present evidence is a classic trigger: “Your eyes are red — have you been crying?”
State verbs stay simple: “I’ve known her for years”, never “I’ve been knowing”.
With “live”, “work” and “study” both forms are possible and mean almost the same: “I’ve lived / I’ve been living here for six years.”
“For” + duration, “since” + starting point — the same pairing you met at node 04.
grammar.deep: This tense is where duration and relevance meet. The perfect part connects the action to now; the continuous part says the action had length and possibly still has. That combination is why it answers “how long?” so naturally and why it so often carries a note of effort or complaint: “I’ve been trying to reach you all morning” contains information about your patience as well as the facts. The clearest way to feel the contrast with the simple perfect is to look at what each one counts. The continuous counts time (“I’ve been reading for two hours”); the simple counts achievements (“I’ve read forty pages”). Both sentences can be true at the same moment, and choosing between them tells your listener whether you want to talk about your effort or your result. One trap: a recently finished activity with visible evidence uses the continuous even though the action has stopped — “It’s been raining” is what you say when the ground is wet and the sky has cleared.

chart.title: Simple or continuous perfect?
rows: I’ve been working here for two years.
You’re dirty — have you been running?
I’ve been going to the gym a lot lately.

examples: I’ve been waiting for the technician since nine and nobody has come.
She’s been learning Portuguese for six months and she’s already reading novels.
Have you been working out? You look great.
We haven’t been getting many complaints lately.
grammar.watch: Never combine the continuous with state verbs, and never with a counted result: “I’ve been writing three emails” should be “I’ve written three emails”.
more: I’ve been waiting for the technician since nine.
She’s been learning Portuguese for six months.
Have you been working out? You look fit.
They haven’t been answering their emails lately.
We’ve been living here since 2019 and we still love it.
My eyes hurt because I’ve been staring at a screen all day.

fix.wrong: I am waiting since nine.
fix.right: I’ve been waiting since nine.
fix.why: Duration up to now needs the perfect, not the present continuous.

fix.wrong: I’ve been reading three books this month.
fix.right: I’ve read three books this month.
fix.why: A counted result takes the simple perfect; the continuous is for the activity.

fix.wrong: She’s been knowing him for years.
fix.right: She’s known him for years.
fix.why: State verbs use the present perfect simple even for duration.

drill.name: How long?
drill.prompt: Answer each question twice: once with “for”, once with “since”, using the present perfect continuous where the verb allows it.

dialogue.line: You look exhausted.
I’ve been preparing the audit since Monday.
How much is left?
I’ve finished four sections. I’ve been working on the last one all morning and it still isn’t right.

contrast.title: Perfect simple or perfect continuous?
rows: I’ve been working here for two years.
We’ve known each other for years.
Have you ever been to Perú?

grammar.sound: “Have been” collapses to /vbɪn/ in connected speech: “I’ve been waiting” sounds like /aɪvbɪnˈweɪtɪŋ/. Only the -ing verb is fully stressed.

speaking.text: Narrate a small accident or surprise. Set the scene in the past continuous, then interrupt it twice with the simple past.
Ask your partner six “How long have you been…?” questions. Every answer must contain “for” or “since” and a continuous form.
One student is a witness, the others ask “What were you doing at…?” for five specific times. The witness must stay consistent.

tips: “When” takes the short event, “while” takes the long background.
Continuous counts time; simple counts results.
State verbs never take a continuous form.

quiz.q: I ___ dinner when the lights went out.
quiz.explain: The background action in progress takes the past continuous; the interruption takes the simple past.

dynamics.name: Freeze frame
dynamics.how: Groups mime a scene and freeze. The class describes what everyone was doing, then the group unfreezes with one sudden event, which the class reports in the simple past.
dynamics.payoff: Makes the background/interruption split physical before it is grammatical.

dynamics.name: Alibi
dynamics.how: Two suspects agree on what they were doing between eight and ten last night, then are questioned separately. The class compares the answers and finds the contradiction.
dynamics.payoff: The classic activity for this tense, and it produces dozens of past continuous questions.

dynamics.name: Since when?
dynamics.how: Each student writes three true facts about ongoing activities without the duration. Others must guess how long, asking “How long have you been…?” until they get within a year.
dynamics.payoff: Question form and duration practice in one loop.

dynamics.name: Simple or continuous
dynamics.how: Teacher reads a context (“Your hands are covered in flour” / “Dinner is on the table”). Teams answer with the right perfect form and justify the choice in five words.
dynamics.payoff: Trains the decision itself rather than the mechanics of the form.

writing.title: The day it went wrong
writing.brief: Narrate an incident. Set the scene in the past continuous, deliver the event in the simple past, and finish with a paragraph in the present perfect continuous about what you have been doing since it happened.
criteria: Three past continuous verbs used as background.
At least one “while” clause and one “when” interruption.
Two present perfect continuous sentences with for or since.

homework.title: Two hours and six months
homework.task: Write six sentences about what you were doing at six specific times yesterday, and six about activities you have been doing for a while, three with “for” and three with “since”. Mark any state verbs and use the simple form for those.

test.q: I ___ home when it started to rain.
test.explain: The background action in progress takes the past continuous.

test.q: While she ___ , the projector failed.
test.explain: “While” introduces the longer action, which is continuous.

test.q: I’ve ___ waiting since nine o’clock.
test.explain: The present perfect continuous is have/has been + -ing.

test.q: She ___ him for twenty years.
test.explain: “Know” is a state verb and takes the perfect simple.

test.q: I’ve ___ four emails this morning.
test.explain: A counted, completed quantity takes the perfect simple.
