units.title: SIGNATURE
units.theme: Describing with participles and identifying with relative pronouns

overview.intro: How do you compress a whole clause into one word in front of a noun? Participles. And how do you attach a defining detail to a person or thing? Relative pronouns. This node covers the -ing / -ed adjective pair and the clauses introduced by who, that and which.
goals: Distinguish present participles (-ing) from past participles (-ed) as adjectives.
Use who, that and which correctly for people and things.
Decide when the relative pronoun can be omitted.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe people, films and situations precisely, and define anything with a relative clause instead of two short sentences.

vocab.def: causing great interest / feeling great interest.
vocab.use: -ing describes the cause, -ed describes the person: “a fascinating book”, “I was fascinated”.
examples: It was a fascinating documentary.
I’m fascinated by how it works.
vocab.colloc: absolutely fascinating · fascinated by

vocab.def: hard to understand / not understanding.
vocab.use: The instructions are confusing; you are confused. Reversing them is the classic mistake.
examples: The form was confusing, so everyone got confused.
I’m confused about the deadline.
vocab.colloc: deeply confused · rather confusing · confused about

vocab.def: worse than expected / feeling let down.
vocab.use: “I was disappointed with the result” — the result was disappointing. Preposition: disappointed with / by / in.
examples: The ending was disappointing.
She was disappointed with her score.
vocab.colloc: deeply disappointed · a disappointing result

vocab.def: making you very tired / feeling very tired.
vocab.use: A day can be exhausting; you are exhausted. Both are strong, so avoid “very”.
examples: It was an exhausting week.
I’m completely exhausted.
vocab.colloc: physically exhausting · utterly exhausted

vocab.def: not working, or in pieces.
vocab.use: Past participles work as adjectives directly before nouns: “a broken screen”, “a locked door”, “a written agreement”.
examples: There’s a broken window in the office.
My phone’s broken.
vocab.colloc: badly broken · a broken promise · broken down

vocab.def: a family member; also “connected to something”.
vocab.use: In grammar, “relative pronoun” means a word that relates a clause to a noun: who, that, which, whose.
examples: A relative of mine lives there.
Relative clauses add information.
vocab.colloc: a close relative · relatively easy

vocab.def: showing possession inside a relative clause.
vocab.use: For people and things: “the man whose car was stolen”, “a company whose profits fell”. Never write “who’s”.
examples: That’s the woman whose son works with me.
We use a system whose interface is terrible.
vocab.colloc: whose name · whose fault

vocab.def: having control or responsibility.
vocab.use: Useful in defining clauses: “the person who is in charge of hiring”.
examples: Who’s in charge here?
The man in charge wasn’t available.
vocab.colloc: in charge of · put in charge

vocab.def: that you can trust to work or to behave well.
vocab.use: For people, machines and sources: “a reliable colleague”, “a reliable source”. Opposite: unreliable.
examples: We need a supplier who is reliable.
The old laptop isn’t reliable any more.
vocab.colloc: highly reliable · a reliable source

vocab.def: making you slightly angry.
vocab.use: The person or thing causing it is annoying; you are annoyed: “an annoying noise”, “I was annoyed”.
examples: That notification sound is really annoying.
He was annoyed about the delay.
vocab.colloc: deeply annoying · get annoyed

vocab.def: to give a particular impression to other people.
vocab.use: Followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: “He comes across as confident.” Usually about unintended impressions.
examples: She comes across as very organised in interviews.
I didn’t mean to come across as rude.
vocab.colloc: come across as friendly · come across badly · come across well

vocab.def: good enough to make people admire it.
vocab.use: An adjective describing the cause, like the -ing participles: the thing is impressive, the person is impressed.
examples: The results were impressive for a first attempt.
It’s an impressive building, but it isn’t practical.
vocab.colloc: deeply impressive · an impressive result · less than impressive

grammar.name: Participles as adjectives: present and past
grammar.short: a boring film / a bored student
grammar.rule: Present participles (-ing) used as adjectives describe the thing that causes a feeling or effect. Past participles (-ed) describe the person or thing that receives it. Past participles are also used to describe a state resulting from an action.
form: -ing = cause: The film was boring. / an interesting idea / a tiring journey.
-ed = experiencer: I was bored. / interested in art / tired after the trip.
Past participle for a resulting state: a broken window, a locked door, a printed form.
Participle before the noun: a fascinating story · a written report.
Participle after the noun (reduced clause): the man standing at the door · the documents signed yesterday.
notes: Only people (and animals) can be “-ed” in the emotional pair, because only they have feelings: a film cannot be bored.
When both are grammatical, the meaning changes completely: “I’m confusing” means you confuse other people.
Prepositions after -ed adjectives are fixed and worth memorising: interested IN, bored WITH/OF, worried ABOUT, surprised AT/BY, disappointed WITH.
Participles after a noun are shortened relative clauses: “the woman who is standing there” → “the woman standing there”.
Past participles as adjectives keep their irregular forms: broken, written, taken, frozen, hidden.
grammar.deep: Once you see the pattern as cause versus effect, the whole family becomes predictable and you stop learning pairs one at a time. The -ing form points outward at the source of a feeling; the -ed form points inward at the experiencer. That is why “I am boring” is a self-criticism and “I am bored” is a complaint about the world. The second half of the topic is subtler and more useful for writing: participles let you compress. Any relative clause with “be” can shrink into a participle phrase — “the people who were waiting outside” becomes “the people waiting outside”, and “the report that was written by the auditor” becomes “the report written by the auditor”. Written English uses this constantly, and using it yourself immediately raises the density of your sentences. Just keep the participle next to the noun it describes: put it too far away and it attaches to the wrong thing, which is how sentences like “I saw the man walking down the street with a telescope” become jokes.
examples: The training was exhausting, and by five everyone was exhausted.
I’m interested in the position, but the description is confusing.
There’s a broken chair and a locked cabinet in the meeting room.
The candidate waiting outside has the strongest CV.
grammar.watch: Things are -ing, people are -ed: “The lecture was boring, so I was bored.”
more: The journey was exhausting and by five everyone was exhausted.
It’s a fascinating idea, but I’m not convinced.
I was surprised by the ending; the whole film was surprising.
There’s a broken window and a locked door on the second floor.
The instructions are confusing, which is why the team looks confused.
She gave a moving speech and half the room was moved.

fix.wrong: I am boring in this class.
fix.right: I am bored in this class.
fix.why: “Bored” describes how you feel; “boring” says you cause the feeling in others.

fix.wrong: The film was very interested.
fix.right: The film was very interesting.
fix.why: The film is the cause, so it takes the -ing form.

fix.wrong: I’m interesting in the job.
fix.right: I’m interested in the job.
fix.why: The person experiences the interest, so the -ed form is required, followed by “in”.

drill.name: Cause or experiencer
drill.prompt: Say each sentence twice: once about the thing, once about the person. Change nothing but the participle.

dialogue.line: How was the training?
Honestly, exhausting. I was exhausted by lunchtime.
Was it useful, though?
Some of it was fascinating. The rest was just confusing, and everyone looked confused.

grammar.sound: Two-syllable -ed adjectives keep the full /ɪd/ ending: “interested” has four syllables in careful speech and three in fast speech, never two.

grammar.name: Relative pronouns for people and things: who, that, which
grammar.short: the woman who called · the file that disappeared
grammar.rule: A defining relative clause tells you which person or thing you mean. “Who” is for people, “which” for things, and “that” for both in defining clauses. The pronoun replaces the subject or the object of the clause — and when it replaces the object, it can be left out.
form: Subject pronoun (cannot be omitted): the man who works upstairs / the app that crashed.
Object pronoun (can be omitted): the man (who/that) I met / the app (that) I downloaded.
Things: the file which / that contains the data.
Possession: the colleague whose laptop was stolen.
Non-defining, with commas, no “that”: My manager, who lives nearby, cycles to work.
notes: Never repeat the subject or object inside the clause: “the man who he called me” and “the book that I read it” are both wrong.
If a noun or pronoun follows the gap, the relative pronoun is an object and can be dropped: “the film I saw”.
In non-defining clauses (extra information, between commas) you must use who or which, never that.
“Where” replaces “in which” for places and “when” replaces “on which” for times: “the office where I work”, “the day when we met”.
Prepositions usually stay at the end in speech: “the person I spoke to”, not “the person to whom I spoke” (formal only).
grammar.deep: Relative clauses are the single most efficient upgrade available to an A2 writer, because they turn two thin sentences into one adult sentence: “I have a colleague. She speaks four languages.” becomes “I have a colleague who speaks four languages.” The mechanics come down to one question — is the relative pronoun doing the subject’s job or the object’s job in its own clause? If it is the subject, it must stay, because a clause without a subject collapses. If it is the object, the clause already has a subject and the pronoun becomes optional, which is why native speakers drop it constantly. The other half of the topic is punctuation, and it carries meaning rather than decoration. “My brother who lives in Bogotá” implies you have more than one brother and identifies him; “My brother, who lives in Bogotá,” implies you have one brother and adds a detail. Commas therefore change the facts, not just the rhythm.
examples: The technician who came yesterday fixed it in ten minutes.
This is the report that everyone is talking about.
The film I watched last night was disappointing.
My neighbour, whose dog barks all night, has finally moved out.
grammar.watch: Do not add an extra pronoun inside the clause: “the book that I read it” must be “the book that I read”.
more: The woman who called yesterday left a number.
That’s the app that keeps crashing.
The colleague whose laptop was stolen is working from home.
This is the file I told you about.
The train that we missed was the last one.
Anyone who wants a copy can email me.

fix.wrong: the man which called
fix.right: the man who called
fix.why: “Which” never refers to a person; use who or that.

fix.wrong: the file that I downloaded it
fix.right: the file that I downloaded
fix.why: The relative pronoun replaces the object; you cannot keep both.

fix.wrong: the woman who’s car broke down
fix.right: the woman whose car broke down
fix.why: Possession takes “whose”; “who’s” is “who is”.

drill.name: Two into one
drill.prompt: Join each pair into a single sentence with a defining relative clause, then say it again dropping the pronoun if that is possible.
items: I met a woman. She works for the ministry.
This is the report. I mentioned it yesterday.
We hired an engineer. His last project failed.
That’s the café. We met there in 2019.
Here’s the key. It opens the back door.

dialogue.line: Who’s the person who signs these off?
The manager whose name is on the header — Ruiz.
Is that the one I emailed last week?
No, that’s the account you contacted. This one’s internal.

grammar.sound: When the pronoun is dropped, the noun and the next subject run together with no pause: “the file I sent”. A pause there signals hesitation, not structure.

speaking.text: Define ten words without saying them, using only relative clauses: “It’s a machine that…”, “It’s a person who…”. Your partner guesses.
Review a film, a course and a restaurant. Each review must use two -ing adjectives and two -ed adjectives correctly.
Describe three people in the room using defining relative clauses only. The group identifies them.

tips: Things are -ing, people are -ed.
Never repeat the subject or object inside a relative clause.
Commas make a relative clause extra information — and then “that” is banned.

quiz.q: The presentation was ___ , so half the audience looked ___ .
quiz.explain: The presentation causes the feeling (-ing); the audience experiences it (-ed).

dynamics.name: Feelings and causes
dynamics.how: One student names a situation, the other produces two sentences: one describing the situation with -ing and one describing their reaction with -ed. Swap after five.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the pair distinction with immediate contrast in every turn.

dynamics.name: Guess who
dynamics.how: Each student writes three defining relative clauses describing a classmate without naming them (“the person who always sits by the window”). Cards are shuffled and read out for the class to guess.
dynamics.payoff: Defining clauses are the only way to win, so the structure is unavoidable.

dynamics.name: Definition auction
dynamics.how: Groups write definitions of five objects using relative clauses (“It’s a thing that…”). Other groups bid on how quickly they can identify each one.
dynamics.payoff: Turns the structure into a game with natural time pressure.

dynamics.name: Whose is it
dynamics.how: Collect one object from each student in a bag. Draw items out and ask the class to build sentences with “whose”: “That’s the student whose pen is green.”
dynamics.payoff: Whose is usually the weakest of the set and needs its own slot.

writing.title: A person worth describing
writing.brief: Describe someone who made an impression on you. Use at least four participle adjectives, correctly split between -ing and -ed, and at least four defining relative clauses to identify people, places and things in the story.
criteria: Four participle adjectives, at least one pair from the same root.
Four defining relative clauses with the correct pronoun.
One clause with whose and one with the pronoun dropped.

homework.title: Pairs and clauses
homework.task: Write eight sentences using four -ing/-ed pairs (both halves of each pair), then rewrite five short pairs of sentences from your own week as single sentences with relative clauses. Mark which pronouns could be dropped.

test.q: The lecture was ___ , so everyone looked ___ .
test.explain: The lecture causes the feeling; the audience experiences it.

test.q: I’m very ___ in the position.
test.explain: The person experiences the interest, so it takes -ed plus “in”.

test.q: That’s the engineer ___ designed the system.
test.explain: A person in subject position takes “who” or “that”.

test.q: The client ___ order was lost called again.
test.explain: Possession takes “whose”.

test.q: This is the file ___ .
options: that I told you about it
test.explain: The object pronoun can be dropped, but the object itself cannot be repeated.

board: Two columns headed THING (-ing) and PERSON (-ed), filled with pairs the class supplies.
Under them, the fixed prepositions: interested IN · worried ABOUT · surprised AT/BY · tired OF.
A relative-pronoun table across the lower half: who · that · which · whose · where.
A rule box: SUBJECT pronoun stays · OBJECT pronoun can go.
Corner error box: “the man which called” and “who’s car”, both crossed out.

units.title: PERMISSIONS
units.theme: How sure you are, and what you are allowed to do

overview.intro: Modals do two jobs in this node. First they measure certainty: from “it must be true” down through “it could be” to “it might not be”. Then they set the rules: what is permitted, what is required, and what is forbidden — the vocabulary of every workplace, airport and building in the world.
goals: Express degrees of certainty with must, may, might and could, plus adverbs.
Ask for and give permission with can, may, could and be allowed to.
State obligation and prohibition accurately with have to, must, mustn’t and can’t.
overview.outcome: By the end you can speculate about an unclear situation at three levels of certainty, and explain the rules of a place without ambiguity.

vocab.def: completely sure.
vocab.use: “I’m certain that…” or “It’s certain to happen”. Slightly stronger and more formal than “sure”.
examples: I’m almost certain she left at five.
There’s no certainty about the date.
vocab.colloc: absolutely certain · a degree of certainty

vocab.def: very likely, but not certain.
vocab.use: Position matters: after “be” but before other verbs — “He’s probably late”, “She probably knows”. With negatives it comes before “won’t”: “He probably won’t come.”
examples: They’ll probably arrive after lunch.
She probably didn’t see the message.
vocab.colloc: most probably · probably not

vocab.def: possibly.
vocab.use: Both usually start the sentence: “Maybe he forgot.” “Maybe” is one word as an adverb; “may be” is a verb form.
examples: Perhaps we should call first.
Maybe it’s a mistake.
vocab.colloc: perhaps not · maybe later

vocab.def: to have permission.
vocab.use: The tensed alternative to “can”: “We weren’t allowed to enter”, “You’ll be allowed to vote”.
examples: Are we allowed to take photos?
I wasn’t allowed to leave early.
vocab.colloc: not allowed to · allowed in · strictly not allowed

vocab.def: not permitted, usually by a rule or law.
vocab.use: Formal register, usually in the passive: “Smoking is strictly prohibited.”
examples: Parking is prohibited here.
Photography is forbidden inside.
vocab.colloc: strictly prohibited · legally forbidden

vocab.def: something you must do.
vocab.use: “Have an obligation to + verb”. The adjective “obligatory” means compulsory.
examples: We have an obligation to report it.
Attendance is obligatory.
vocab.colloc: a legal obligation · under no obligation

vocab.def: to accept something as true without checking.
vocab.use: Followed by a that-clause: “I assumed you knew.” Central to speculation.
examples: I assumed the meeting was cancelled.
Don’t assume anything.
vocab.colloc: safe to assume · a reasonable assumption

vocab.def: facts that show something is true.
vocab.use: Noncount: “some evidence”, “a piece of evidence”, never “evidences”.
examples: There’s no evidence that he took it.
The evidence suggests otherwise.
vocab.colloc: clear evidence · lack of evidence · based on evidence

vocab.def: expected to, according to a rule or an arrangement.
vocab.use: “We’re supposed to wear ID.” In the past it often implies failure: “I was supposed to call her.”
examples: You’re supposed to check in online.
We were supposed to start at nine.
vocab.colloc: supposed to be · not supposed to

vocab.def: probably not going to happen or be true.
vocab.use: “It’s unlikely (that)…” or “be unlikely to + verb”: “He’s unlikely to agree.”
examples: It’s unlikely that they’ll finish today.
An unlikely explanation.
vocab.colloc: highly unlikely · unlikely to happen

vocab.def: to work out the answer to something by thinking about it.
vocab.use: Separable: “figure it out”. Common with question words: “I can’t figure out why it failed.”
examples: We still haven’t figured out what caused the outage.
Give me a minute — I’ll figure it out.
vocab.colloc: figure out why · figure it out · hard to figure out

vocab.def: in a way that must be obeyed exactly.
vocab.use: Common in rules and notices: “Entry is strictly prohibited.” Also softens into “strictly speaking”.
examples: Photography is strictly forbidden in the archive.
Strictly speaking, you need written permission.
vocab.colloc: strictly prohibited · strictly speaking · strictly necessary

grammar.name: Modals and adverbs for degrees of certainty
grammar.short: It must be broken. It might be the cable. It can’t be the software.
grammar.rule: When you deduce rather than know, English uses modals to show how sure you are. “Must” is a confident conclusion, “may / might / could” are open possibilities, and “can’t / couldn’t” is a confident negative conclusion. Adverbs do the same job in a different position.
form: Near certainty (positive): must + base verb → She must be at lunch.
Possibility: may / might / could + base verb → It might be a network problem.
Near certainty (negative): can’t / couldn’t + base verb → He can’t be serious.
Adverbs: definitely, certainly, probably, possibly, maybe, perhaps → It’s definitely the cable.
Continuous form: must / might + be + -ing → They must be waiting outside.
notes: The negative of deductive “must” is “can’t”, not “mustn’t”: “He can’t be at home” (deduction) vs “He mustn’t be at home” (prohibition).
“May not” and “might not” express a real possibility that something is untrue: “She might not know yet.”
“Could” in speculation means possible, but “can” does not: never “It can be the cable” for speculation.
Adverb position: “definitely / probably / certainly” go after “be” but before other verbs, and before a negative auxiliary — “He definitely isn’t coming.”
For deductions about the past, add “have + participle”: “She must have forgotten” — a preview of node 15.
grammar.deep: Speculation is a scale, and modal verbs are the marks along it. At the top, “must” means you have evidence and have drawn a conclusion — not that you know for a fact, which is an important nuance: “She must be tired” actually means “I deduce she is tired.” In the middle, “may”, “might” and “could” are almost interchangeable, with “may” a little more formal and “could” a little more casual. At the bottom, English does something asymmetrical that catches learners out: the negative conclusion is not “mustn’t” but “can’t”, because “mustn’t” has already been claimed by prohibition. Keep the two ladders separate in your head — one for deduction (must / might / can’t), one for rules (must / can / mustn’t) — and remember that the same word can be on both ladders with different meanings, which is exactly why context and intonation do so much work in real speech.

chart.title: Certainty scale
rows: It might not be the router.

examples: Nobody’s answering — they must be in the meeting.
It might be a permissions problem, or it could just be the cache.
That can’t be right; the numbers don’t add up.
She probably won’t reply before Monday.
grammar.watch: For a negative deduction use “can’t”, not “mustn’t”: “He can’t be the manager” (I deduce he isn’t).
more: The lights are on, so someone must be working late.
It might be the cable, or it could be the port.
That can’t be the right invoice — the date is wrong.
She may not have seen the message yet.
He must know about it; he was in the meeting.
It could easily be a permissions problem.

fix.wrong: He mustn’t be the manager; he looks too young.
fix.right: He can’t be the manager; he looks too young.
fix.why: A negative deduction takes “can’t”; “mustn’t” means prohibition.

fix.wrong: It must to be broken.
fix.right: It must be broken.
fix.why: Modals are followed by the bare infinitive.

fix.wrong: Maybe it can be the router.
fix.right: It might be the router.
fix.why: “Can” expresses ability or general possibility, not a specific guess.

drill.name: Read the evidence
drill.prompt: Give two deductions for each situation: one confident with must or can’t, one tentative with might or could.
items: the office lights are still on at ten
the shop is closed on a Tuesday

dialogue.line: Nobody’s answering the support line.
They must be dealing with the outage.
Or the line might be down too.
It can’t be down — I called it an hour ago and it rang.

grammar.sound: Modals of deduction are unstressed; the stress falls on the content word: “It must be BROken.” Stressing “must” turns the deduction into insistence.

grammar.name: Permission, obligation and prohibition
grammar.short: You can park here. You have to pay. You mustn’t smoke.
grammar.rule: Three separate ideas, three sets of forms. Permission uses can, may, could and be allowed to. Obligation uses must, have to, need to and be supposed to. Prohibition uses mustn’t, can’t and is not allowed to. The negatives are not interchangeable.
form: Permission: You can / may use this room. / Are we allowed to record?
Asking permission: Can I…? Could I…? May I…? (most formal) / Would it be all right if I…?
Obligation: You must sign in. / You have to wear a badge. / Everyone needs to register.
No obligation: You don’t have to stay. / You needn’t worry.
Prohibition: You mustn’t open that. / You can’t park here. / Recording is not allowed.
notes: “Don’t have to” = optional; “mustn’t” = forbidden. This distinction decides whether your rule makes sense.
“May” is the most formal permission form and appears in notices: “Visitors may use the side entrance.”
Only “have to”, “be allowed to” and “be supposed to” can change tense: “We weren’t allowed to enter”, “You’ll have to wait”.
“Can’t” often replaces “mustn’t” in speech for prohibition: “You can’t take photos in here.”
“Be supposed to” describes an expectation rather than a hard rule, and in the past it usually implies the rule was broken: “I was supposed to send it yesterday.”
grammar.deep: Rules are social, so the form you choose sends a message about your authority as well as the content of the rule. “You must submit the form” sounds like the speaker owns the rule; “you have to submit the form” sounds like they are reporting someone else’s; “you’re supposed to submit the form” sounds like a reminder that also leaves room for the fact that you did not. Learn the pairs by their negatives, because that is where meaning flips rather than fades — must / mustn’t, have to / don’t have to, can / can’t, be allowed to / not be allowed to. And note which forms are grammatically complete: true modals cannot conjugate, so any rule you need to put into the past or the future has to be expressed with “have to” or “be allowed to”. That is why real-world English uses those two far more than “must”, which survives mostly in written notices and in the deduction sense you met in the previous topic.

chart.title: Rules toolkit
rows: You may leave your bag here.
Can I / Could I / May I
You have to show your ticket.
We’re supposed to arrive by nine.

examples: You can bring a guest, but they have to sign in at reception.
You mustn’t leave the door open — it locks automatically.
Are we allowed to eat at our desks? — You can, but you don’t have to hide it.
We were supposed to finish by six, so we had to stay late.
grammar.watch: “You don’t have to come” invites; “You mustn’t come” forbids. Choose carefully.
more: You can park here after six.
Visitors have to sign in at reception.
You mustn’t use your phone during the exam.
We don’t have to be there before ten.
Are we allowed to record the session?
You’re supposed to wear a badge, but nobody checks.

fix.wrong: You mustn’t come if you don’t want — it’s optional.
fix.right: You don’t have to come if you don’t want — it’s optional.
fix.why: “Mustn’t” forbids; “don’t have to” removes the obligation.

fix.wrong: Can I to leave early?
fix.right: Can I leave early?
fix.why: Modals take the bare infinitive.

fix.wrong: We must to pay before Friday.
fix.right: We have to pay before Friday.
fix.why: “Must” takes no “to”, and an external rule is more naturally “have to”.

drill.name: Rules of the place
drill.prompt: For each place, give one permission, one obligation and one prohibition, using a different structure each time.

dialogue.line: Am I allowed to bring a guest?
You can, but they have to sign in at the desk.
Do I need to tell you in advance?
You don’t have to, though it helps. And they mustn’t go past the second floor.

contrast.title: Obligation and its opposites
rows: You don’t have to pay today.
You’re supposed to wear a badge.

grammar.sound: “Have to” is pronounced /hæftə/ and “has to” /hæstə/, with an /f/ and an /s/. “Mustn’t” drops the first t entirely: /ˈmʌsnt/.

speaking.text: Look at three photos of unclear situations. Each student offers one deduction with “must”, one possibility with “might” and one rejection with “can’t”.
Choose a place you know. State ten rules using can, can’t, have to, don’t have to and mustn’t. The group flags any rule that is ambiguous.
Ask your teacher, your boss and your best friend for the same favour, changing the level of formality each time.

tips: Two ladders: deduction (must / might / can’t) and rules (must / can / mustn’t).
“Don’t have to” is freedom; “mustn’t” is prohibition.
Only “have to” and “be allowed to” can move through the tenses.

quiz.q: The lights are off and the door is locked. They ___ have gone home.
quiz.explain: The evidence supports a confident conclusion, so “must” expresses the deduction.

dynamics.name: Evidence table
dynamics.how: Each group gets a photo of a room or a bag of objects and writes six deductions, ranked from most to least certain. They then defend the ranking to another group.
dynamics.payoff: The ranking makes the scale of certainty explicit instead of accidental.

dynamics.name: House rules
dynamics.how: Pairs invent a place (a co-working space, a hostel, a lab) and write eight rules: two permissions, three obligations, two prohibitions, one “supposed to”. Other pairs guess the place.
dynamics.payoff: Forces the full modal set rather than the two students already know.

dynamics.name: Must or mustn’t
dynamics.how: Teacher reads situations; students hold up MUST / MUSTN’T / DON’T HAVE TO cards. Every mismatch is discussed on the spot.
dynamics.payoff: Targets the highest-frequency error in the node.

dynamics.name: Twenty deductions
dynamics.how: One student thinks of an object in their bag. The class asks yes/no questions and must phrase each guess as a deduction: “It could be…”, “It must be…”, “It can’t be…”.
dynamics.payoff: Repeats the structures dozens of times in a single game.

writing.title: The rules and the mystery
writing.brief: Part one: explain the rules of a place you know well, using permission, obligation and prohibition at least twice each. Part two: describe an unexplained situation from your week and give three deductions about it at different levels of certainty.
criteria: Six modal structures of permission, obligation and prohibition, correctly distinguished.
Three deductions using must, might/could and can’t.
No “to” after must, and no “mustn’t” where “don’t have to” is meant.

homework.title: Certainty and rules
homework.task: Write six deductions about photographs or situations you saw today, one for each point on the certainty scale, then list eight rules from your workplace or school split into must / have to / mustn’t / don’t have to.

test.q: The car isn’t here, so she ___ have left already.
test.explain: The evidence supports a confident positive conclusion.

test.q: That ___ be Ana — she’s in Lima this week.
test.explain: A negative deduction takes “can’t”.

test.q: You ___ pay now; you can do it online later.
test.explain: The obligation is absent, not the permission.

test.q: Visitors ___ sign in at reception.
test.explain: An external rule takes “have to” plus the base verb.

test.q: It ___ be the cable, but I’m not sure.
test.explain: An open possibility takes might, may or could.

board: A vertical thermometer down the left edge: MUST at the top, MIGHT / COULD in the middle, CAN’T at the bottom.
Beside each mark, the matching adverb: definitely · almost certainly · possibly · probably not.
On the right, three stacked boxes: CAN / ALLOWED TO — HAVE TO / MUST — MUSTN’T / NOT ALLOWED.
Between the last two, a wide arrow labelled DON’T HAVE TO = no obligation, NOT prohibition.
Corner error box: “must to be” and “mustn’t be the manager”, both crossed out.

units.title: ROLLBACK
units.theme: Imaginary situations and things you should have done differently

overview.intro: The unreal past, in two directions. The second conditional imagines a present or future that is not true, and past modals judge decisions that are already made. Both take a step back in tense to signal that we have left reality — the same move you learnt with “wish”.
goals: Build second conditional sentences with if + past simple and would + base verb.
Use should have, shouldn’t have and would have to comment on past actions.
Distinguish real (first) from unreal (second) conditionals.
overview.outcome: By the end you can argue a hypothetical case (“if I were in charge…”) and review a past decision with regret, blame or justification.

vocab.def: to feel sorry about something you did or didn’t do.
vocab.use: “Regret + -ing” for the past action (“I regret sending it”); “regret + to inform” is a formal announcement of bad news.
examples: I regret not taking that job.
We regret to inform you that the position is filled.
vocab.colloc: deeply regret · no regrets · regret doing

vocab.def: to say that someone is responsible for something bad.
vocab.use: “Blame someone for something” or “blame something on someone”. “To be to blame” = to be responsible.
examples: Don’t blame me for the delay.
Nobody was to blame.
vocab.colloc: take the blame · blame it on · who’s to blame

vocab.def: in your situation.
vocab.use: The classic second conditional opener: “If I were in your shoes, I’d resign.”
examples: If I were in your shoes, I’d wait.
I wouldn’t like to be in his shoes.
vocab.colloc: in your shoes · put yourself in my shoes

vocab.def: to refuse an offer; also to reduce volume.
vocab.use: Separable: “turn down the offer”, “turn it down”. Common in regret sentences.
examples: I turned down the job and I still regret it.
Could you turn it down a bit?
vocab.colloc: turn down an offer · turn down the volume

vocab.def: if not; in the other case.
vocab.use: Links a condition to a consequence across two sentences: “Leave now; otherwise you’ll miss it.”
examples: Write it down, otherwise you’ll forget.
She apologised; otherwise I would have complained.
vocab.colloc: otherwise fine · or otherwise

vocab.def: imagined, not real.
vocab.use: “A hypothetical situation” — the exact label for second conditional content. Noun: hypothesis.
examples: Let’s take a hypothetical case.
That’s purely hypothetical.
vocab.colloc: a hypothetical question · purely hypothetical

vocab.def: justified by the result.
vocab.use: Frequent in evaluating past decisions: “It wouldn’t have been worth it.”
examples: The extra cost wasn’t worth it.
It would have been worth trying.
vocab.colloc: worth the risk · not worth it

vocab.def: to tell someone about a risk in advance.
vocab.use: “I warned you” is the natural companion of “you should have listened”.
examples: I warned you about that supplier.
They warned us not to click the link.
vocab.colloc: warn someone about · fair warning

vocab.def: something you learn from an experience.
vocab.use: “Learn a lesson”, “that taught me a lesson”. Useful for closing a regret story.
examples: It was an expensive lesson.
I learnt my lesson.
vocab.colloc: a hard lesson · learn a lesson

vocab.def: in place of.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “instead of waiting”, never an infinitive.
examples: I should have called instead of sending an email.
Instead of complaining, do something.
vocab.colloc: instead of that · rather than

vocab.def: looking back now, with knowledge you did not have then.
vocab.use: Opens a sentence of regret and pairs naturally with “should have”: “In hindsight, I should have waited.”
examples: In hindsight, we accepted too quickly.
It was obvious in hindsight.
vocab.colloc: in hindsight · with hindsight · hindsight is easy

grammar.name: Unreal conditional sentences with if clauses (second conditional)
grammar.short: If I had more time, I would travel.
grammar.rule: The second conditional describes an imaginary present or future: a situation that is not true, is unlikely, or is purely hypothetical. The if-clause takes the past simple, and the main clause takes would (or could / might) plus the base verb.
form: If + past simple, would + base verb → If I earned more, I would move out.
Reversed: I would move out if I earned more.
With “to be”: If I were you… (were for all persons in careful English).
Other modals: If we left now, we could still catch it. / she might agree.
Negative: If I didn’t have to work, I wouldn’t stay in the city.
notes: The past tense here is unreal, not past: “If I had a car” is about now.
“If I were you, I would…” is the standard way to give strong advice in English.
Never put “would” in the if-clause of a standard second conditional: “If I would have time” is wrong.
Contrast with the first conditional: “If it rains, I’ll stay in” (real possibility) vs “If it rained in July, everyone would be surprised” (unlikely).
“Could” in the main clause means ability or possibility; “might” means the result itself is uncertain.
grammar.deep: Second conditionals are the grammar of argument and imagination, and they behave exactly like “wish”: one step back in tense equals one step away from reality. The past form is a marker of unreality, which is why “if I were” survives as a subjunctive form here even though English has lost most of its subjunctive elsewhere. Two practical uses make this structure worth mastering. First, advice: “if I were you” lets you tell someone what to do while explicitly acknowledging that you are not them, which is why it lands so much more gently than “you should”. Second, negotiation and speculation: “if we cut the budget, we would lose the third phase” puts a consequence on the table without committing to it. Keep the two conditionals distinct by asking whether you consider the condition realistic. If yes, use the first; if you are imagining, use the second. And keep “would” out of the if-clause — the only place it belongs is the result.

chart.title: First vs second conditional
rows: If I get the job, I’ll move.
If I got the job, I’d move.
If he is late, we’ll start.
If he were late, we’d start.
If I were you, I’d wait.

examples: If I spoke better English, I would apply for that position.
What would you do if your laptop died the night before the deadline?
If I were you, I’d talk to her before Monday.
We could finish today if we didn’t have so many meetings.
grammar.watch: No “would” after “if”: “If I had time, I would help” — never “If I would have time”.
more: If I had more time, I’d learn another language.
What would you do if you lost your phone abroad?
If I were you, I’d ask for it in writing.
We would move closer to the office if the rent weren’t so high.
If she spoke Portuguese, she’d get the Brazil account.
I wouldn’t take that job even if they doubled the salary.

fix.wrong: If I would have more time, I would travel.
fix.right: If I had more time, I would travel.
fix.why: “Would” never appears in the if-clause.

fix.wrong: If I was you, I’d wait.
fix.right: If I were you, I’d wait.
fix.why: In this fixed advice pattern careful English uses “were” for all persons.

fix.wrong: If I win the lottery, I would buy a house.
fix.right: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
fix.why: The two halves must match: unreal condition, unreal result.

drill.name: Unreal chain
drill.prompt: Answer each question with a full second conditional, then turn your answer into the next question for your partner.
items: if you had a free year
if you had to move tomorrow
if money were not a factor

dialogue.line: Would you take the transfer if they offered it?
If it were permanent, yes. As a six-month trial, no.
What would you do about the flat?
I’d rent it out. If I sold it, I couldn’t afford to come back.

contrast.title: First against second conditional
rows: If it rains, we’ll stay in.
If it rained, we’d stay in.

grammar.sound: “Would” contracts to /d/ on the pronoun — “I’d”, “she’d”, “we’d” — and is almost inaudible. Without the contraction the sentence sounds like a first conditional.

grammar.name: Past modals: should have and would have
grammar.short: I should have called. / I would have helped.
grammar.rule: To comment on the past, English adds “have + past participle” to a modal. “Should have” expresses regret, criticism or an unfulfilled expectation. “Would have” expresses what was hypothetically possible in a past that did not happen — the result half of a third conditional.
form: should have + participle → I should have booked earlier. (I didn’t.)
shouldn’t have + participle → You shouldn’t have said that. (You did.)
would have + participle → I would have helped, but nobody told me.
could have + participle → We could have won. (We didn’t.)
Third conditional: If I had known, I would have called.
notes: The pattern is always modal + have + participle, never “should had” or “should of” — the last one is a spelling of the spoken contraction “should’ve” and is always wrong in writing.
“Should have” criticises the past; “should” alone advises the present: “You should call her” vs “You should have called her”.
“Would have” usually needs a condition, stated or implied: “I would have come (if I had known).”
“Must have” is deduction about the past (“she must have left”), not obligation — see node 14.
In speech these contract heavily: should’ve, would’ve, could’ve, must’ve. Train your ear for them.
grammar.deep: Past modals let you talk about roads not taken, which is why they carry so much emotional weight. “I should have listened” admits fault. “You shouldn’t have told him” assigns it. “I would have helped” defends your intention against the facts. Structurally they are simple — the modal never changes, “have” never changes, and the only variable is the participle — but they are difficult to hear, because in real speech the whole cluster reduces to a single unstressed syllable. Training your ear here pays off twice: it fixes your listening and it stops you writing “should of”. Notice too how naturally they combine with the third conditional to complete the conditional system: node 09 gave you the real future, this node gives you the unreal present and the unreal past. “If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train” is the last piece — a fact that cannot be changed, discussed as if it could.

chart.title: Past modal meanings
rows: If I’d known, I’d have called.

examples: I should have backed up the file before the update.
You shouldn’t have paid in cash — now there’s no record.
I would have told you, but your phone was off.
We could have avoided all this if we had read the contract.
grammar.watch: Write “should have” (or “should’ve”), never “should of”, and never “should had”.
more: I should have booked the tickets earlier.
You shouldn’t have told him before the meeting.
I would have helped if you had asked me.
We should have left ten minutes ago.
She wouldn’t have signed it without reading it.
They should have warned us about the road closure.

fix.wrong: I should booked earlier.
fix.right: I should have booked earlier.
fix.why: Past modals need “have” plus the past participle.

fix.wrong: I should have went.
fix.right: I should have gone.
fix.why: After “have” the verb takes the participle, not the past simple.

fix.wrong: You should have not said that.
fix.right: You shouldn’t have said that.
fix.why: The negative attaches to the modal, not to “have”.

drill.name: Second thoughts
drill.prompt: For each situation, give one criticism with “should have” and one alternative with “would have”.
items: the team sent the wrong file

dialogue.line: They gave the contract to the other agency.
We should have sent the proposal on Monday.
Would it have made a difference?
Probably. I would have called them too, in hindsight.

contrast.title: Talking about the past you cannot change
rows: We could have taken the train.
I would help, but I’m busy.

grammar.sound: “Have” reduces to /əv/ and attaches to the modal: “should’ve” /ˈʃʊdəv/, “would’ve” /ˈwʊdəv/. That is why learners write “should of” — the sound is identical, the spelling is not.

speaking.text: Bring a real dilemma. Each classmate advises you with “If I were you, I’d…” and one “you should have…” about what led you here.
Describe three hypothetical versions of your life with second conditionals. Your partner asks one follow-up question about each.
In groups, review a failed plan (real or invented). Each person contributes one “should have”, one “could have” and one “would have”.

tips: Unreal = one step back in tense. Present unreal → past; past unreal → past perfect.
“Would” lives in the result clause only.
Modal + have + participle. Never “should of”.

quiz.q: If I ___ you, I wouldn’t sign anything today.
quiz.explain: The second conditional takes a past form in the if-clause, and “were” is the standard form for all persons in “if I were you”.

dynamics.name: Impossible dilemmas
dynamics.how: Each group gets four dilemma cards and must reach a group answer for each, in full second conditionals. Every member speaks at least twice per card.
dynamics.payoff: Genuine disagreement produces long unreal sentences instead of short ones.

dynamics.name: Advice clinic
dynamics.how: Half the class present a real minor problem; the other half give advice, always starting “If I were you, I’d…”. Rotate three times, then the advisers report the best advice they gave.
dynamics.payoff: Drills the fixed pattern in the situation where it actually occurs.

dynamics.name: Post-mortem
dynamics.how: Groups read a short account of a project that failed and write six sentences about what should have happened, then two about what would have happened instead.
dynamics.payoff: Forces both past modals in a context where they are the natural response.

dynamics.name: Should have / should of
dynamics.how: Teacher dictates eight sentences at natural speed. Students write them and compare; every “should of” on a page is corrected by its writer at the board.
dynamics.payoff: Attacks the spelling error at the point where it is created.

writing.title: A decision I would change
writing.brief: Write about a decision you or someone you know made. Part one: what you would do if you were in that situation now, in second conditionals. Part two: what should have happened, using past modals.
criteria: Four second conditionals, none with “would” after “if”.
One “If I were you” sentence.
Three past modals with have + past participle, spelled correctly.

homework.title: Unreal and undone
homework.task: Write six second conditionals about your own life and six sentences with should have, shouldn’t have or would have about last month. Circle every past participle and check it is not a past simple form.

test.q: If I ___ more time, I’d take the course.
test.explain: The second conditional takes the past simple in the if-clause.

test.q: If I ___ you, I’d wait until Monday.
test.explain: “Were” is standard for all persons in this advice pattern.

test.q: We ___ have booked earlier; now everything is full.
test.explain: “Should have” expresses regret about a past omission.

test.q: You shouldn’t ___ told her before the announcement.
test.explain: The structure is modal + have + past participle; “of” is a spelling error.

test.q: I ___ have helped if you had asked.
test.explain: “Would have” describes an unreal past result.

A note beside the unreal line: past form = distance from reality, not past time.
Lower half headed THE PAST YOU CAN’T CHANGE: should have · shouldn’t have · would have · could have · must have.
Under it, the pronunciation box: should’ve /ˈʃʊdəv/ — never “should of”.
Corner error box: “If I would have time” crossed out twice.

units.title: RELAY
units.theme: Passing on what other people said and asked for

overview.intro: The final node is about transmission: taking someone’s words and delivering them in your own. Reported speech shifts tenses back, changes pronouns and time words, and turns requests into infinitives. Master it and you can relay a conversation accurately, which is the highest-value skill in any workplace.
goals: Report statements with said, told and that, applying the tense backshift.
Report requests and commands with asked / told + object + to + infinitive.
Adjust pronouns, time and place words when the context changes.
overview.outcome: By the end you can listen to a short conversation and report it accurately in three sentences, without quoting.

vocab.def: to give information to a specific person.
vocab.use: “Tell” always needs a person: “tell me”, “tell her”. Compare “say”, which does not: “She said that…”.
examples: She told me she was leaving.
Tell them we’ll be late.
vocab.colloc: tell the truth · tell someone about · tell a story

vocab.def: to speak words.
vocab.use: “Say (that) + clause”, with no person, unless you add “to”: “He said to me that…” (less common).
examples: He said he would call back.
What did she say?
vocab.colloc: say sorry · say nothing · as I said

vocab.def: to say something briefly, without detail.
vocab.use: “Mention that…” or “mention + noun”. No person object without “to”: “He mentioned it to me.”
examples: She mentioned that the deadline moved.
Nobody mentioned the budget.
vocab.colloc: briefly mention · not to mention · as mentioned

vocab.def: to say you are unhappy about something.
vocab.use: “Complain (to someone) about something” or “complain that…”. Common in reported speech.
examples: He complained that the room was too cold.
She complained to HR about the schedule.
vocab.colloc: complain about · a formal complaint

vocab.def: to say something firmly and repeatedly.
vocab.use: “Insist on + -ing” or “insist that + clause”: “She insisted on paying.”
examples: He insisted that he had sent it.
She insisted on seeing the manager.
vocab.colloc: insist on · strongly insist

vocab.def: to accept that something bad is true.
vocab.use: “Admit + -ing” or “admit that…”: “He admitted making a mistake.” Never an infinitive.
examples: She admitted that she had forgotten.
He admitted breaking the rule.
vocab.colloc: admit a mistake · freely admit

vocab.def: to say you will definitely do something.
vocab.use: “Promise to + verb” or “promise that…”: “He promised to send it today.”
examples: They promised to call back within an hour.
She promised she wouldn’t tell anyone.
vocab.colloc: break a promise · keep a promise

vocab.def: to say no to something.
vocab.use: “Refuse to + verb”, never -ing: “He refused to sign.” Noun: refusal.
examples: She refused to give her name.
They refused our request.
vocab.colloc: flatly refuse · refuse to accept

vocab.def: to make someone remember something.
vocab.use: “Remind someone to + verb” (a task) or “remind someone about + noun”. Not the same as “remember”, which is your own memory.
examples: Remind me to send the invoice.
She reminded us about the meeting.
vocab.colloc: remind me to · a gentle reminder

vocab.def: according to what people say; it seems.
vocab.use: A useful way to report information you have not verified: “Apparently they’re closing the office.”
examples: Apparently, the flight was cancelled.
She’s leaving, apparently.
vocab.colloc: apparently not · apparently so

vocab.def: to tell someone about a fact they may not have noticed.
vocab.use: A reporting verb in its own right: “She pointed out that the date was wrong.” Separable with objects.
examples: He pointed out that we had already paid.
Someone pointed out the mistake before we sent it.
vocab.colloc: point out that · point out a problem · as I pointed out

vocab.def: used to restate something more simply or more directly.
vocab.use: Introduces a reformulation, which is exactly what reporting is: “In other words, she said no.”
examples: The budget is frozen. In other words, we can’t hire.
In other words, they want it by Friday.
vocab.colloc: in other words · to put it another way · that is to say

grammar.name: Reported speech: statements
grammar.short: “I’m tired.” → She said she was tired.
grammar.rule: When you report what someone said, the verb usually moves one tense back, the pronouns change to your point of view, and time and place words shift to match your situation. “Say” takes no personal object; “tell” requires one.
form: Present → past: “I work here.” → He said he worked there.
Present continuous → past continuous: “I’m waiting.” → She said she was waiting.
Past simple → past perfect: “I saw it.” → He said he had seen it.
will → would; can → could; must → had to → “I’ll call.” → She said she would call.
Structure: said (that) + clause / told + person + (that) + clause.
notes: “That” is optional after both verbs: “She said (that) she was busy.”
No backshift is necessary when the information is still true or the reporting is immediate: “She says she’s on her way.”
Pronouns and possessives shift with the speaker: “I lost my keys” → He said he had lost his keys.
Time and place words shift too: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.
“Say” cannot take a person directly: “He said me” is wrong; use “He told me” or “He said to me”.
grammar.deep: Reported speech looks like a table of transformations, but underneath it there is a single logic: you are re-anchoring the utterance to your own here and now. The original speaker’s present is in your past, so the tense moves back; their “I” is your “he”; their “tomorrow” may already be yesterday by the time you report it. Once you think of it as re-anchoring rather than memorising, the exceptions make sense too — if nothing has moved (you are reporting a general truth, or the words were spoken a minute ago) then nothing needs to shift: “She says the office closes at six.” The past perfect deserves a note: it is the end of the road backwards, so a past simple and a past perfect original both report as a past perfect, and in relaxed speech many speakers leave a past simple unchanged when the sequence is already clear. Finally, choose your reporting verb deliberately. “Said”, “told”, “explained”, “admitted”, “complained” and “insisted” report the same words while telling your listener what kind of act it was — and that choice is often more informative than the words themselves.

chart.title: Backshift table
rows: “I live here.” → She said she lived there.
“I’m working.” → He said he was working.
“I called.” → She said she had called.
“I’ve finished.” → He said he had finished.
“I’ll help.” → She said she would help.
“I can’t come.” → He said he couldn’t come.

examples: “The system is down.” → The technician said the system was down.
“I’ll send it tomorrow.” → She told me she would send it the next day.
“I didn’t receive your email.” → He said he hadn’t received my email.
“We’re still hiring.” → They say they’re still hiring. (still true, no backshift)
grammar.watch: “Say” never takes a person object: “She told me…” or “She said that…”, never “She said me…”.
more: “The system is down.” → The technician said the system was down.
“I’ll call you tomorrow.” → She told me she would call me the next day.
“We’ve already paid.” → He said they had already paid.
“I can’t come on Friday.” → She said she couldn’t come on Friday.
“I saw her yesterday.” → He said he had seen her the day before.
“I’m working from home today.” → She said she was working from home that day.

fix.wrong: She said me she was tired.
fix.right: She told me she was tired.
fix.why: “Say” takes no person object; “tell” requires one.

fix.wrong: He said that he is busy.
fix.right: He said that he was busy.
fix.why: The reported verb moves one tense back after a past reporting verb.

fix.wrong: She said she will call me tomorrow.
fix.right: She said she would call me the next day.
fix.why: “Will” backshifts to “would”, and “tomorrow” shifts with it.

drill.name: One step back
drill.prompt: Report each quotation with “said” or “told me”, shifting the tense, the pronouns and the time word.
items: “I’ve been waiting here for an hour.”

dialogue.line: What did the client say?
She said the budget had been approved.
And the timeline?
She told me they wanted it the following week. In other words, we start on Monday.

grammar.sound: “Said” is /sed/, not /seɪd/, and “told” keeps a clear /l/. In connected speech “said that” often loses “that” entirely, which is perfectly correct.

grammar.name: Reported speech: requests and commands
grammar.short: “Please wait.” → She asked me to wait.
grammar.rule: Requests, orders and advice are not reported with a that-clause but with an object plus an infinitive. The reporting verb carries the force: asked (request), told (order), advised, reminded, warned, invited, begged.
form: Request: asked + object + to + verb → She asked me to wait outside.
Order: told + object + to + verb → He told us to be quiet.
Negative: asked / told + object + not to + verb → She asked me not to call after nine.
Other verbs: advised / reminded / warned / invited / encouraged + object + to + verb.
Reported questions: asked + if / whether or wh-word, with statement order → He asked if I was free. / She asked where I lived.
notes: The negative goes before “to”: “not to be late”, never “to not be late” in careful English.
These verbs all need a personal object: “She asked to wait” means she wanted to wait herself, which is a different meaning.
Reported questions lose their inversion and their “do”: “Where do you work?” → She asked where I worked.
“Say” cannot report a request: “He said me to wait” is wrong — use “told me to wait”.
Choose the verb for the force of the original: “told” sounds like an order, “asked” like a request, “begged” like desperation.
grammar.deep: This structure is where reported speech becomes genuinely useful, because most of what we relay in working life is not information but instructions. The infinitive pattern is elegantly economical: “She asked me to resend the invoice” contains the speaker, the addressee, the action and the social force of the original in eight words. The single most common error is dropping the object — English insists on knowing who was asked — and the second is choosing a verb that misrepresents the force, which can create real friction: reporting your colleague’s polite “could you check this?” as “he told me to check it” makes them sound rude. Note the parallel with reported questions, which drop inversion and auxiliaries in exactly the way indirect questions did at node 02; the same principle is at work, because an embedded clause is never a question in its own right. Together, these two topics close the level: you can now carry other people’s words, requests and questions across time and person without quoting them.

chart.title: Reporting different speech acts
rows: She asked me to wait there.
He told us to be quiet.
She told me not to touch it.
She asked if I was free.

examples: “Could you send the file again?” → She asked me to send the file again.
“Don’t forget the deadline.” → He reminded us not to forget the deadline.
“Have you finished?” → She asked whether I had finished.
“Come to the meeting at four.” → They invited me to come to the meeting at four.
grammar.watch: Requests need an object and an infinitive: “asked me to wait”. And the negative is “not to”, never “to not”.
more: “Please wait here.” → She asked me to wait there.
“Be quiet!” → He told us to be quiet.
“Don’t forget the deadline.” → She reminded us not to forget the deadline.
“Could you send it again?” → He asked me to send it again.
“You should see a doctor.” → She advised me to see a doctor.
“Don’t touch the settings.” → They told us not to touch the settings.

fix.wrong: She asked to wait outside.
fix.right: She asked me to wait outside.
fix.why: Without an object this means she wanted to wait herself.

fix.wrong: He told to us to be quiet.
fix.right: He told us to be quiet.
fix.why: “Tell” takes a direct object with no preposition.

fix.wrong: She asked me to not be late.
fix.right: She asked me not to be late.
fix.why: The negative goes before “to” in careful English.

drill.name: Instruction relay
drill.prompt: Report each instruction with the reporting verb that fits its force: asked, told, advised, reminded or warned.

dialogue.line: Did you speak to reception?
Yes. They asked me to sign in and told me to wear a badge.
Anything else?
They warned us not to use the back stairs, and reminded me to return the badge at six.

contrast.title: Reporting different speech acts
rows: He told us to be quiet.
He reminded me not to forget.
She warned me not to touch it.
He asked if I was coming.

grammar.sound: “Asked” keeps its cluster, /ɑːskt/, and “told us” links into /ˈtəʊldəs/. Dropping the final consonant makes the reporting verb ambiguous.

speaking.text: In threes: A whispers three sentences to B, B reports them to C, C checks the original. Score one point per accurate backshift.
Take four phone messages from your partner and report them to the class: two statements, one request, one question.
Report the same statement with three different verbs (said, complained, insisted) and discuss how the meaning changes.

tips: Report by re-anchoring: tense back one step, pronouns to your point of view, time words to your clock.
“Tell” needs a person, “say” does not.
Requests take “asked/told + object + to + verb”, and the negative is “not to”.

quiz.q: “Please don’t tell anyone.” → She asked me ___ anyone.
quiz.explain: Reported requests use “asked + object + to + infinitive”, and the negative goes before “to”: not to tell.

dynamics.name: Whispers, scored
dynamics.how: A whispers three sentences to B, who reports them to C, who reports them to D. D writes them down and the group compares with the original, scoring one point per correct backshift.
dynamics.payoff: Every transmission forces the shift, and the scoring makes accuracy matter.

dynamics.name: Message pad
dynamics.how: Students take four phone messages from a partner reading from a card, then report all four to a third student. Two must be statements, one a request, one a question.
dynamics.payoff: Reproduces the real-life situation reported speech exists for.

dynamics.name: Verb of force
dynamics.how: Groups report the same original sentence with five different verbs (said, insisted, complained, admitted, warned) and rank them by how strong they sound.
dynamics.payoff: Moves students past “said” and shows that the verb carries the meaning.

dynamics.name: Interview relay
dynamics.how: Each student interviews one classmate with three questions, then reports the answers to a second classmate, who reports them to the class. Errors are corrected only at the final stage.
dynamics.payoff: Two layers of reporting expose whether the backshift is automatic yet.

writing.title: What they told me
writing.brief: Report a real conversation you had this week. Include at least four reported statements with backshift and three reported requests or instructions, using at least three different reporting verbs.
criteria: Four reported statements with correct backshift and pronoun changes.
Three object + infinitive structures, one of them negative.
At least three different reporting verbs, and no “said me”.

homework.title: Ten quotations
homework.task: Collect ten things people said to you today. Report five as statements with backshift and five as requests, orders or advice with an object and an infinitive. Note the time and place words you had to change.

test.q: She ___ me she was tired.
test.explain: A person object requires “tell”.

test.q: “I’ll call you tomorrow.” → He said he ___ call me the next day.
test.explain: “Will” backshifts to “would”.

test.q: “Please wait outside.” → She asked me ___ outside.
test.explain: Requests take object + to + infinitive.

test.q: “Don’t be late.” → He told us ___ late.
test.explain: The negative goes before “to”.

test.q: “I saw her yesterday.” → He said he ___ her the day before.
test.explain: The past simple backshifts to the past perfect.
